q: Which of the following is the best example of the entity theory of partnership?
o: Partners co-own specific partnership property as "tenants in partnership."
A partnership dissolves whenever any partner leaves the firm.
A partnership may sue, be sued, and own property in its own name.
Partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations.
None of the above.
oe: That is the UPA (1914) aggregate rule (§ 25). Under RUPA § 501 a partner is not a co-owner of partnership property.
That is the UPA aggregate approach (§§ 29, 31). RUPA replaces it with dissociation, which need not dissolve the firm.
Correct. RUPA § 201: "A partnership is an entity distinct from its partners." It sues and is sued (§ 307) and owns property (§ 203) as an entity.
Personal liability of partners is an aggregate leftover that survives in RUPA § 306; it is not what makes RUPA an entity statute.
C states the entity theory.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Entity vs. aggregate theory

q: Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), which of the following events results in a partner's dissociation?
o: The partner's death.
The partner's transfer of his entire transferable interest in the partnership.
The partner's expulsion in accordance with the partnership agreement.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True: death is a dissociation event (§ 601).
False. A transfer is not a dissociation; the transferor stays a partner. A transfer of the whole interest only gives the other partners a ground to expel him unanimously (§ 601(4)).
True: expulsion under the agreement is a dissociation event (§ 601(3)).
Correct. Death and expulsion under the agreement dissociate; a transfer of one's interest does not.
B is wrong: transferring a transferable interest is not dissociation.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Dissociation events

q: Which of the following is NOT required for a principal to ratify an agent's unauthorized act?
o: The principal knew, or had reason to know, the material facts.
The principal communicated the affirmance to the third party in writing.
The act was done, or purported to be done, on the principal's behalf.
The principal affirms the entire transaction.
The third party had not withdrawn from the transaction before the affirmance.
oe: Required. Ratification needs knowledge of all material facts (Ercanbrack; R3d § 4.06).
Correct: this is NOT required. Ratification may be express or implied, most commonly by knowingly accepting benefits, and even by silence where there is a duty to speak.
Required (R3d § 4.03; Botticello: the husband never claimed to act for his wife).
Required. There is no partial ratification (R3d § 4.07).
Required. Ratification is ineffective if the third party has already withdrawn (R3d § 4.05).
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification requirements

q: In Gorton v. Doty, the court held that the coach who drove the teacher's car to the football game was the teacher's agent, even though:
o: The coach was not paid.
There was no written agreement between them.
The teacher did not direct how the coach drove the car.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Consideration and payment are not required for agency; a gratuitous agent is still an agent.
True. Agency rests on consent, not on a contract or writing.
True. Control can be minimal: naming the driver was enough. The right to control, not its actual exercise, matters.
Incomplete. C is also true.
Correct. A gratuitous favor with one condition (only the coach may drive) supplied consent and control. No pay, no contract, and no detailed control were needed.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Gorton v. Doty

q: Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), a partner's transferable interest consists of:
o: The partner's right to receive distributions.
The partner's share of specific partnership property.
The partner's right to participate in management.
The partner's right to inspect the partnership's books and records.
All of the above.
oe: Correct. The transferable interest is the right to receive distributions (§ 102). A transferee gets that and nothing else.
A partner has no interest in specific partnership property under RUPA; the entity owns it (§ 501).
Management rights stay with the partner and do not pass with a transfer.
Information rights belong to partners, not transferees.
Only A is part of the transferable interest.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Transferable interest

q: Which of the following business forms requires NO filing with the state to be created?
o: A limited liability partnership (LLP).
A limited partnership (LP).
A limited liability company (LLC).
A general partnership.
A limited liability limited partnership (LLLP).
oe: An LLP requires filing a statement of qualification.
An LP is formed only when a certificate of limited partnership is filed.
An LLC is formed by filing a certificate (articles) of organization.
Correct. A general partnership needs no state action; it forms whenever two or more persons carry on as co-owners a business for profit, even inadvertently.
An LLLP is an LP that elects that status in its filed certificate.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dana, Eli, and Farah are partners in Harbor Lights, a general partnership that owns and operates a bakery and café. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "No partner may purchase equipment costing more than $10,000 without the written consent of all partners." "Profits shall be divided 50% to Dana, 25% to Eli, and 25% to Farah." The agreement says nothing about how long the partnership will last or how losses are shared.

Eli, without telling Dana or Farah, buys a $14,000 commercial oven from Ovenworks, Inc. on the partnership's credit, signing the contract "Harbor Lights, by Eli, partner." Ovenworks does not know about the $10,000 limit in the partnership agreement. Is the partnership bound to pay Ovenworks?
o: No, because third parties are charged with knowing the partnership agreement.
Yes, because buying an oven is in the ordinary course, and Ovenworks had no notice of the limit.
Yes, but only because Eli signed in the partnership's name rather than his own.
No, because a purchase over $10,000 is outside the ordinary course.
None of the above.
oe: Third parties have no duty to read the partnership agreement (RNR Investments). Without knowledge or notice, the private limit does not bind Ovenworks.

Correct. RUPA § 301: a partner's ordinary-course act binds the partnership unless the partner lacked authority AND the third party knew or had notice of it. The agreement limits Eli's actual authority, not his apparent authority.
The form of signature is not the test; an ordinary-course act binds whether written or oral.
The $10,000 cap is an internal limit, not a measure of what is ordinary. Buying ovens is plainly the ordinary business of a bakery.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Ordinary-course authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dana, Eli, and Farah are partners in Harbor Lights, a general partnership that owns and operates a bakery and café. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "No partner may purchase equipment costing more than $10,000 without the written consent of all partners." "Profits shall be divided 50% to Dana, 25% to Eli, and 25% to Farah." The agreement says nothing about how long the partnership will last or how losses are shared.

Assume the partnership pays Ovenworks. As among the partners, which of the following statements is true?
o: Eli must indemnify the partnership for loss caused by his breach.
Eli has no liability, because the partnership is bound to Ovenworks.
Dana and Farah may treat the contract with Ovenworks as void.
Eli is automatically dissociated for breaching the partnership agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The partnership is bound to the third party, but a partner who exceeds actual authority is liable to the partnership for loss caused by his breach of the agreement (§ 410(a)).
Binding the firm externally does not excuse the internal breach.
The contract binds the partnership; the remedy is against Eli, not Ovenworks.
A breach is not an automatic dissociation event. At most it may support judicial expulsion if it is willful or persistent and material (§ 601(5)).
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Exceeding actual authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dana, Eli, and Farah are partners in Harbor Lights, a general partnership that owns and operates a bakery and café. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "No partner may purchase equipment costing more than $10,000 without the written consent of all partners." "Profits shall be divided 50% to Dana, 25% to Eli, and 25% to Farah." The agreement says nothing about how long the partnership will last or how losses are shared.

In Year 2, the partnership loses $40,000. How will the loss be shared among the partners?
o: Equally, about $13,333 each, because losses are shared per capita.
In proportion to each partner's capital contribution to the firm.
$20,000, $10,000, and $10,000, because losses follow the profit shares.
Dana bears the full loss because she receives the largest share of profits.
None of the above.
oe: Per-capita sharing is the default only for profits when nothing is agreed. Here the agreement sets profit shares.
Capital contributions do not set loss shares by default.
Correct. Absent agreement, each partner is chargeable with a share of losses in proportion to that partner's share of profits (RUPA § 401; UPA § 18(a)).
No rule puts the whole loss on the largest profit-sharer.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Default loss sharing

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dana, Eli, and Farah are partners in Harbor Lights, a general partnership that owns and operates a bakery and café. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "No partner may purchase equipment costing more than $10,000 without the written consent of all partners." "Profits shall be divided 50% to Dana, 25% to Eli, and 25% to Farah." The agreement says nothing about how long the partnership will last or how losses are shared.

Farah tells Dana and Eli in writing that she is "done" and withdraws from the partnership. Under the RUPA, which of the following statements is true?
o: Farah's withdrawal is wrongful because she gave no advance notice to the others.
Farah's withdrawal triggers a mandatory Article 7 buyout while Dana and Eli continue the business.
Farah is not dissociated until Dana and Eli consent to her leaving.
Farah is dissociated, and her withdrawal dissolves the at-will partnership.
None of the above.
oe: There is no term and no agreed notice requirement, so withdrawal by express will is not wrongful (§ 602(b)).
In an at-will partnership, a partner's express will to withdraw causes dissolution, not a buyout (§ 801(1)), unless the partners agree otherwise.
A partner always has the power to dissociate by express will (§ 602(a)).
Correct. The agreement states no term, so the partnership is at will, and § 801(1) makes a partner's express will to withdraw a dissolution event.
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — At-will withdrawal

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Dana, Eli, and Farah are partners in Harbor Lights, a general partnership that owns and operates a bakery and café. Their written partnership agreement includes the following provisions: "This partnership is governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) except as this agreement provides." "No partner may purchase equipment costing more than $10,000 without the written consent of all partners." "Profits shall be divided 50% to Dana, 25% to Eli, and 25% to Farah." The agreement says nothing about how long the partnership will last or how losses are shared.

Dana handles purchasing. A flour supplier tells her that the café space next door is available for lease, an ideal spot for a second Harbor Lights location. Dana leases the space herself and opens her own café there without telling Eli or Farah. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Dana breached her duty of loyalty and must account for her profits.
Dana committed no breach, because her conduct merely furthered her own interest.
Dana breached only the duty of care, by failing to tell her partners.
Dana committed no breach unless the agreement expressly prohibits competition.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 409(b): a partner must hold as trustee any benefit from appropriating a partnership opportunity and must refrain from competing before dissolution. She learned of it through her partnership role (Meinhard).
That rule (§ 409(e)) does not excuse taking an opportunity that belongs to the partnership or competing with it.
This is a loyalty problem. Care covers gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct, and knowing violations of law.
The duty not to compete is a statutory default; the agreement would have to authorize the activity, not forbid it.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Partnership opportunity

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ruth owns the Maple Court apartment building. She hires Victor as resident manager under a written agreement: "Victor will collect rents, show units, and arrange routine repairs." Ruth separately tells Victor, in private, "Do not sign any service contract longer than one year without asking me first." The sign at the entrance reads "Maple Court — Managed by Victor Lane." For the past three springs, Victor has hired GreenCo Landscaping for the season, and Ruth has paid every invoice without comment.

The written agreement says nothing about cleaning. Victor hires a part-time janitor to clean the hallways, as resident managers of similar buildings customarily do. What kind of authority did Victor have?
o: Express actual authority.
Apparent authority only.
Implied actual authority.
Inherent agency power only.
None of the above; Victor had no authority.
oe: Nothing in the agreement or Ruth's instructions mentions janitors.
Apparent authority looks to the third party's belief. Here the agent himself reasonably believed he was authorized, which is actual authority.
Correct. Hiring a janitor is incidental to managing a building and customary for the position, so Victor reasonably understood he was authorized (the apartment-manager hypo; Mill Street).
Inherent authority is a fallback when there is no actual or apparent authority. Analyze actual authority first.
Custom and the incidents of the job supply implied actual authority.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Implied actual authority

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ruth owns the Maple Court apartment building. She hires Victor as resident manager under a written agreement: "Victor will collect rents, show units, and arrange routine repairs." Ruth separately tells Victor, in private, "Do not sign any service contract longer than one year without asking me first." The sign at the entrance reads "Maple Court — Managed by Victor Lane." For the past three springs, Victor has hired GreenCo Landscaping for the season, and Ruth has paid every invoice without comment.

Victor signs a three-year landscaping contract with GreenCo in Ruth's name. GreenCo does not know about Ruth's one-year instruction. After the first year, Ruth refuses to pay. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Ruth is bound, because Victor had express actual authority to arrange landscaping.
Ruth is not bound, because an agent's own conduct can't create apparent authority.
Ruth is bound only if she later ratifies the full three-year term.
Ruth is bound, because her own manifestations gave Victor apparent authority.
None of the above.
oe: Ruth's private instruction forbade contracts over one year, so Victor lacked actual authority for this one.
The second half is a correct rule, but here the manifestation comes from Ruth herself: the position, the sign, and her payment of prior contracts.
No ratification is needed if apparent authority exists.

Correct. By placing Victor in the manager's position, posting the sign, and paying his past landscaping contracts, Ruth manifested to GreenCo that he was authorized, and GreenCo reasonably believed it. Apparent authority must be traceable to the principal's manifestations (R3d § 3.03), and a secret limit does not bind a third party without notice.
D is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Apparent authority from position

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ruth owns the Maple Court apartment building. She hires Victor as resident manager under a written agreement: "Victor will collect rents, show units, and arrange routine repairs." Ruth separately tells Victor, in private, "Do not sign any service contract longer than one year without asking me first." The sign at the entrance reads "Maple Court — Managed by Victor Lane." For the past three springs, Victor has hired GreenCo Landscaping for the season, and Ruth has paid every invoice without comment.

Ruth fires Victor on June 1 but tells no one. On June 10, Victor orders $2,000 of mulch from GreenCo on Ruth's account. GreenCo has no reason to know Victor was fired. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Termination of Victor's actual authority automatically ended his apparent authority.
Ruth may be bound, because Victor's apparent authority lingers.
Ruth is not bound, because Victor's firing was effective against everyone on June 1.
Victor cannot be liable to GreenCo, because he purported to act for Ruth.
None of the above.
oe: Terminating actual authority does not automatically end apparent authority.
Correct. Apparent authority ends when it is no longer reasonable for the third party to believe the agent is authorized. Ruth could have cut it off by notifying GreenCo.
The firing ended actual authority between Ruth and Victor, not GreenCo's reasonable reliance.
If Ruth were not bound, Victor would be liable to GreenCo on the implied warranty of authority (R3d § 6.10).
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Lingering apparent authority

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ruth owns the Maple Court apartment building. She hires Victor as resident manager under a written agreement: "Victor will collect rents, show units, and arrange routine repairs." Ruth separately tells Victor, in private, "Do not sign any service contract longer than one year without asking me first." The sign at the entrance reads "Maple Court — Managed by Victor Lane." For the past three springs, Victor has hired GreenCo Landscaping for the season, and Ruth has paid every invoice without comment.

While he was still manager, Victor secretly accepted a $1,500 "referral fee" from GreenCo for steering the landscaping contract to it. GreenCo's price was fair, and Ruth suffered no loss. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Victor must account to Ruth for the $1,500.
Ruth may terminate Victor and may withhold his compensation for the period of his intentional breach.
Victor may keep the fee, because Ruth suffered no loss.
Victor breached only the duty of care.
A and B.
oe: True. An agent may not acquire a material benefit from a third party in connection with the agency (R3d § 8.02). The remedy is disgorgement even without loss to the principal (Reading v. Regem).
True. Withholding compensation for intentional breaches is among the remedies for breach of fiduciary duty.
Loss is irrelevant. Loyalty means no profiting from the position.
A secret profit from the agency is a breach of loyalty.
Correct. Victor must disgorge the secret profit, and Ruth may terminate him and withhold his pay for the period of the breach.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Secret referral fee

q: Under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), a person admitted as a partner into an existing partnership is:
o: Personally liable for all partnership obligations, including earlier ones.
Not personally liable for pre-admission debts, though the partner's contribution is at risk.
Not liable for any partnership obligation until one year after admission.
Liable for pre-admission obligations only if the partner knew of them.
None of the above.
oe: RUPA § 306(b) protects incoming partners from personal liability for pre-admission obligations.
Correct. § 306(b): an incoming partner is not personally liable for obligations incurred before admission. The partner's investment in the firm is still at risk.
No such waiting period exists. The partner is personally liable for obligations incurred after admission.
Knowledge does not matter; the rule is categorical.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Incoming partner liability

q: Under the RUPA (1997), which of the following, standing alone, raises a presumption that a person is a partner in a business?
o: Co-ownership of property as joint tenants, with profits from it shared.
Sharing the gross returns of a venture, whether or not the parties share property.
Receiving a share of profits as wages for work done for the business.
Receiving a share of profits other than as wages, rent, interest, or debt repayment.
None of the above.
oe: Co-ownership does not by itself establish a partnership, even if profits from the property are shared (§ 202(c)(1)).
Sharing gross returns does not by itself establish a partnership (§ 202(c)(2)).
Profits received as wages fall within an exception and raise no presumption (Fenwick).

Correct. § 202(c)(3): profit sharing creates a presumption of partnership unless the profits were received as repayment of a debt, wages, rent, an annuity or retirement benefit, interest on a loan, or the price of goodwill or other property.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Profit-sharing presumption

q: Which of the following best describes the difference between apparent authority and estoppel?
o: Apparent authority requires a manifestation by the principal, while estoppel requires no conduct by the principal at all.
Apparent authority binds both sides to the contract; estoppel only compensates the third party's reliance.
Estoppel binds both the principal and the third party to the contract, like apparent authority.
Apparent authority requires proof of a detrimental change of position in every jurisdiction.
None of the above.
oe: Estoppel also requires principal conduct: the principal intentionally or carelessly caused the belief, or failed to correct it (R3d § 2.05).

Correct. Apparent authority makes the principal and the third party parties to the contract. Estoppel only protects a third party who detrimentally changed position, and compensates that reliance loss.
Estoppel runs one way: it protects the relying third party but does not bind that third party to the contract.
Apparent authority requires a reasonable belief; only some courts also require a change of position. Detrimental reliance is the hallmark of estoppel.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Apparent authority vs. estoppel

q: Under the Restatement (Third) of Agency, a principal is DIRECTLY liable for an agent's tort in which of the following situations?
o: The principal was negligent in selecting, training, retaining, or supervising the agent.
The agent acted with actual authority, and the conduct is tortious.
An employee committed the tort within the scope of employment.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True: direct liability (R3d §§ 7.03(1), 7.05).
True: direct liability (R3d § 7.03(1)(a)).
That is respondeat superior, a form of VICARIOUS liability (§§ 7.03(2), 7.07).
Correct. Negligent selection or supervision, and torts committed with actual authority, are direct liability; scope-of-employment liability is vicarious.
C describes vicarious, not direct, liability.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Direct vs. vicarious liability

q: Under the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA) in the statutory supplement, which of the following statements is true?
o: A member is an agent of the LLC solely by reason of being a member, as in a partnership.
Failure to observe formalities is a ground for imposing personal liability on members.
By default, an LLC is member-managed, and membership alone creates no personal liability.
A member who withdraws is entitled to have the LLC buy out the member's interest at fair value.
None of the above.
oe: Under § 301, a member is NOT an agent solely by reason of being a member. Partners are automatic agents; members are not.
Section 304 says the opposite.
Correct. Member-management is the default, and § 304 shields members and managers from company obligations solely by reason of their status.
The ULLCA has no mandatory buyout; a dissociated member keeps only a transferee's economic interest.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — LLC basics

q: In Kovacik v. Reed, the court held that:
o: Where one partner gave only money and the other only services, each loses his own contribution.
Losses are shared in the same proportion as profits, so the service partner owed half of the capital loss.
The service partner had to reimburse half the loss because he agreed to share profits equally.
Losses are shared in proportion to each partner's capital contribution.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. "Upon loss of the money the party who contributed it is not entitled to recover any part of it from the party who contributed only services."
That is the statutory result under UPA § 18(a), which Kovacik declined to apply.
The court reasoned the reverse: an equal profit split implied that money and labor were valued equally, so each lost his own contribution.
That is one possible rule but not Kovacik's holding.
A states the holding.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Kovacik holding

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Valley Grain Co. is a small grain elevator that buys grain from local farmers. To keep Valley running, Midland Foods Corp. gives Valley a growing line of credit and buys 90% of Valley's grain. In return, Valley must obtain Midland's approval before making capital improvements, paying dividends, or encumbering its assets. Midland's regional manager visits Valley weekly, criticizes its management, and supplies Valley with Midland-printed forms. The written agreement between them states, "Valley is an independent contractor and not an agent of Midland." Valley collapses owing local farmers $900,000 for grain.

The unpaid farmers sue Midland. Can they recover?
o: No, because the agreement states that Valley is not Midland's agent, and the parties' label controls.
No, because a creditor that protects its loan with veto rights can never be a principal.
Yes, because Midland's control and course of dealing made it Valley's principal.
Yes, but only if Midland expressly agreed to answer for Valley's debts to farmers.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control; agency is judged by the parties' actual conduct (R3d § 1.02; MJ & Partners).
A creditor that crosses from protecting its loan to running the debtor's business becomes a principal (R2d § 14O).

Correct. These are the A. Gay Jenson Farms v. Cargill facts: consent, acting for Midland, and de facto control shown by the course of dealing make Midland a principal liable for Valley's grain purchases.
Agency can arise from conduct without any intent to be liable.
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Creditor as principal (Cargill)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Valley Grain Co. is a small grain elevator that buys grain from local farmers. To keep Valley running, Midland Foods Corp. gives Valley a growing line of credit and buys 90% of Valley's grain. In return, Valley must obtain Midland's approval before making capital improvements, paying dividends, or encumbering its assets. Midland's regional manager visits Valley weekly, criticizes its management, and supplies Valley with Midland-printed forms. The written agreement between them states, "Valley is an independent contractor and not an agent of Midland." Valley collapses owing local farmers $900,000 for grain.

Midland argues that it was merely a lender, like the lenders in Martin v. Peyton. Which fact, if true, would BEST support Midland's argument?
o: Midland could veto risky deals but couldn't initiate deals or bind Valley.
Midland's manager told Valley each day which contracts to make with farmers.
Valley used purchase forms printed with Midland's name and logo.
Midland's manager criticized Valley's management and practices every week.
All of the above.
oe: Correct. In Martin v. Peyton the lenders could veto but not initiate or bind. Protective rights that do not amount to running the business point toward lender status.
Directing daily operations is exactly what made Cargill a principal.
Supplying its own forms was one of the Cargill control factors.
Ongoing criticism and oversight cut toward control.
Only A supports lender status.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Lender vs. principal

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Valley Grain Co. is a small grain elevator that buys grain from local farmers. To keep Valley running, Midland Foods Corp. gives Valley a growing line of credit and buys 90% of Valley's grain. In return, Valley must obtain Midland's approval before making capital improvements, paying dividends, or encumbering its assets. Midland's regional manager visits Valley weekly, criticizes its management, and supplies Valley with Midland-printed forms. The written agreement between them states, "Valley is an independent contractor and not an agent of Midland." Valley collapses owing local farmers $900,000 for grain.

In deciding whether Valley acted as Midland's agent, a court applies the elements of agency. Which of the following is NOT one of those elements?
o: A manifestation by the principal that the agent will act for it.
The agent's acceptance of the undertaking.
An understanding that the principal will be in control of the undertaking.
A writing evidencing the agency relationship.
None of the above; all are elements.
oe: This is an element (Botticello; R2d § 1).
This is an element.
This is an element.
Correct: this is NOT an element. A writing is generally not required, except where the agent will sign contracts within the Statute of Frauds.
D is not an element.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Elements of agency

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Valley Grain Co. is a small grain elevator that buys grain from local farmers. To keep Valley running, Midland Foods Corp. gives Valley a growing line of credit and buys 90% of Valley's grain. In return, Valley must obtain Midland's approval before making capital improvements, paying dividends, or encumbering its assets. Midland's regional manager visits Valley weekly, criticizes its management, and supplies Valley with Midland-printed forms. The written agreement between them states, "Valley is an independent contractor and not an agent of Midland." Valley collapses owing local farmers $900,000 for grain.

Suppose instead that Midland simply bought Valley's grain at market prices and had no veto, oversight, or financing role. Midland would most likely be treated as:
o: Valley's principal, because it buys most of Valley's output.
Valley's partner, because their profits depend on each other.
A guarantor of Valley's debts to the farmers who sold it grain.
A buyer, not a principal, because it bought and resold for its own account.
None of the above.
oe: Being a major customer is not control of the business.
Nothing suggests co-ownership or shared profits of a single business.
Nothing creates a guaranty.

Correct. R2d § 14K: one who buys goods and resells them for its own account is not an agent unless the parties agree it acts for the buyer. In Cargill, Warren was no independent supplier because of Cargill's control.
D is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Supplier vs. agent (§ 14K)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Valley Grain Co. is a small grain elevator that buys grain from local farmers. To keep Valley running, Midland Foods Corp. gives Valley a growing line of credit and buys 90% of Valley's grain. In return, Valley must obtain Midland's approval before making capital improvements, paying dividends, or encumbering its assets. Midland's regional manager visits Valley weekly, criticizes its management, and supplies Valley with Midland-printed forms. The written agreement between them states, "Valley is an independent contractor and not an agent of Midland." Valley collapses owing local farmers $900,000 for grain.

As Midland's transactional lawyer at the start of the relationship, which step would have BEST reduced Midland's risk of Cargill-style liability?
o: Adding stronger and more detailed "not an agent" disclaimers to the agreement.
Limiting Midland to protective vetoes and covenants, and staying out of daily operations.
Supplying Valley with more Midland-branded forms to show Midland's involvement.
Having Midland's manager review and approve each of Valley's purchases from farmers.
None of the above.
oe: Labels are informative but not dispositive; the Cargill court looked past them.

Correct. Information rights, ordinary loan covenants, and vetoes that protect an investment are safe. The line is between protecting an investment (Martin v. Peyton) and running the business (Cargill).
That adds evidence of control.
Approving each transaction is day-to-day control.
B is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Transactional planning

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Grace and Hector agree to open a craft brewery. Grace contributes $100,000 in cash and wants no role in daily operations. Hector contributes no money but will run the brewery full time. They want Grace to have limited liability. They sign a document titled "Limited Partnership Agreement" naming Hector the general partner and Grace the limited partner, and agree that profits will be split 60% to Grace and 40% to Hector.

Before anyone files anything with the state, the brewery buys $30,000 of hops on credit and cannot pay. Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding Grace's liability?
o: Grace is liable only up to her $100,000 contribution, because the agreement names her a limited partner.
No certificate was filed, so they are general partners, and Grace may be personally liable.
Grace is not liable for any debts, because she contributed only capital and no services.
Grace is liable only if she participated in managing the brewery's business.
None of the above.
oe: A private agreement cannot create limited liability. An LP exists only when its certificate is filed.
Correct. Co-owners sharing profits form a general partnership by default (RUPA § 202), and an LP is formed only by filing a certificate.
Contributing capital rather than services does not shield a general partner.
The control question is irrelevant when no LP exists.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — No certificate filed

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Grace and Hector agree to open a craft brewery. Grace contributes $100,000 in cash and wants no role in daily operations. Hector contributes no money but will run the brewery full time. They want Grace to have limited liability. They sign a document titled "Limited Partnership Agreement" naming Hector the general partner and Grace the limited partner, and agree that profits will be split 60% to Grace and 40% to Hector.

Now assume they properly filed a certificate of limited partnership naming Hector the general partner and Grace the limited partner. Grace begins attending weekly management meetings and voting on major purchases. Under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001), which of the following statements is true?
o: Grace loses her limited liability because she participated in control of the business.
Grace becomes a general partner by operation of law because of her role.
Grace keeps her limited liability despite participating in management.
Grace is liable only to creditors who knew she participated in management.
None of the above.
oe: That was the old "control rule," which ULPA (2001) § 303 largely eliminated.
Participating in management does not convert a limited partner into a general partner.
Correct. ULPA (2001) § 303: a limited partner is not liable for the LP's obligations even if the limited partner participates in management and control.
That reflects older versions of the act, not ULPA (2001).
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Control rule abolished

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Grace and Hector agree to open a craft brewery. Grace contributes $100,000 in cash and wants no role in daily operations. Hector contributes no money but will run the brewery full time. They want Grace to have limited liability. They sign a document titled "Limited Partnership Agreement" naming Hector the general partner and Grace the limited partner, and agree that profits will be split 60% to Grace and 40% to Hector.

In the properly formed limited partnership, Hector, the general partner, is:
o: Personally liable for the LP's debts, unless the LP elected LLLP status.
Liable only to the extent of his capital contribution.
Not liable, because he contributed no capital.
Liable only for his own torts.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. General partners manage and have full personal liability. LLLP status shields them too.
That describes a limited partner.
A general partner's liability does not depend on his contribution.
A general partner answers for the LP's obligations generally.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — General partner liability

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Grace and Hector agree to open a craft brewery. Grace contributes $100,000 in cash and wants no role in daily operations. Hector contributes no money but will run the brewery full time. They want Grace to have limited liability. They sign a document titled "Limited Partnership Agreement" naming Hector the general partner and Grace the limited partner, and agree that profits will be split 60% to Grace and 40% to Hector.

Grace and Hector want to protect Hector from personal liability while keeping the limited partnership structure. Which of the following would accomplish that goal?
o: Electing limited liability limited partnership (LLLP) status in the filed certificate.
Forming a corporation to serve as the sole general partner.
Adding a clause to the partnership agreement stating that Hector is not personally liable to third parties.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. An LLLP shields general partners as well as limited partners.
True. A corporate general partner is the common structure that gives everyone in an LP limited liability (Frigidaire), subject to veil piercing.
False. An internal agreement cannot bind outside creditors.
Correct. LLLP status and a corporate general partner both work; a private clause does not.
C does not protect Hector against creditors.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Shielding the general partner

q: Under both the UPA (1914) and the RUPA (1997), a partnership is formed by:
o: Filing a statement of partnership authority with the secretary of state's office.
Two or more persons carrying on as co-owners a business for profit, intended or not.
A written agreement signed by all of the partners and filed locally.
The parties' express agreement that they intend to be partners.
B and D.
oe: No filing is needed to form a general partnership.
Correct. RUPA § 202(a); UPA § 6. No formalities are needed, and a partnership can be formed inadvertently.
No writing is required.
Subjective intent to be "partners" is not required; intent to do the things that make a partnership is enough.
D is wrong.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Formation standard

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the requirements under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 228 for conduct to be within the scope of employment?
o: The conduct is of the kind the employee is employed to perform.
The conduct occurs substantially within the authorized time and space limits.
The conduct is actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the employer.
The employer expressly authorized the specific act.
If force is intentionally used, its use is not unexpectable by the employer.
oe: This is a § 228 requirement.
This is a § 228 requirement.
This is a § 228 requirement.
Correct: this is NOT required. Even forbidden acts can be within scope (R2d § 230).
This is a § 228 requirement.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — R2d § 228 elements

q: Under RUPA § 409, a partner's duty of care to the partnership and the other partners is limited to refraining from:
o: Ordinary negligence.
Grossly negligent or reckless conduct.
Intentional misconduct.
A knowing violation of law.
B, C and D.
oe: Ordinary negligence is NOT a breach of a partner's duty of care.
Part of the duty.
Part of the duty.
Part of the duty.
Correct. The care duty covers gross negligence or recklessness, intentional misconduct, and knowing violations of law, but not ordinary negligence.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Partner duty of care

q: In Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission, the court held that the receptionist was an employee rather than a partner primarily because:
o: The written agreement called her a partner, which the court treated as decisive.
She received 20% of the profits rather than a fixed salary.
In substance, she lacked the marks of a co-owner, and her profit share was wages.
She could not read the partnership agreement she signed.
None of the above.
oe: The court looked past the label, which favored her being a partner anyway.
Profit sharing would ordinarily suggest partnership; the court held these profits were really wages.

Correct. She contributed no capital, had no control, and shared no losses. Weighing intent, profit and loss sharing, ownership, control, conduct toward others, and rights on dissolution, co-ownership was missing.
That was the partner in Zajac v. Harris, who was held to be a partner.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Fenwick

q: Watteau v. Fenwick is the classic example of:
o: Inherent agency power binding an undisclosed principal despite secret limits.
Apparent authority arising from the position the brewers gave the manager.
Estoppel based on the supplier's reliance on the manager.
Ratification of the cigar purchases by the brewers' later conduct.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The brewers forbade the manager to buy cigars, but they were bound because buying cigars was within the authority usually given to such a manager (R2d §§ 194–195).
The supplier had never heard of the brewers, so there was no manifestation by the principal to the third party.
The supplier did not rely on any belief created by the brewers.
The brewers repudiated the purchase.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Watteau v. Fenwick

q: Which of the following is generally the most appropriate way to fund a buyout triggered by a partner's death?
o: Disability insurance.
A pension or 401(k) plan.
Life insurance.
A property settlement in divorce.
None of the above.
oe: Disability insurance funds disability-triggered buyouts.
Retirement plans fund retirement buyouts.
Correct. Death is funded with life insurance, retirement with a pension or 401(k), and disability with disability insurance.
Divorce is a separate trigger to plan for, not a funding source for death.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Funding a buyout

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ivan owns Spoke & Chain, a struggling bicycle shop. His friend Jade lends him $60,000. Their written "Loan Agreement" says Jade will receive 30% of the shop's profits until she has received $90,000, may inspect the books monthly, and may veto any single purchase over $15,000. Kurt has worked at the shop for years; Ivan agrees to pay him a salary plus a bonus of 10% of profits. Ivan also lets his cousin Lena, a well-known local cyclist, tell suppliers that she is "Ivan's partner in Spoke & Chain." Lena has no ownership interest in the shop.

Is Jade a partner in Spoke & Chain?
o: Yes, because sharing profits is conclusive evidence of a partnership between Jade and Ivan.
Yes, because her veto power over large purchases gives her control of the business.
No, because loan repayment from profits raises no presumption, and her rights protect a lender.
No, because the parties called it a "Loan Agreement," and that label controls.
None of the above.
oe: Profit sharing only raises a presumption, and not when profits are received as repayment of a loan or interest.
A veto over large purchases protects a lender's investment; it is not the power to run the business.

Correct. Profits received as repayment of a loan do not raise the presumption of partnership, and her information and veto rights are reasonable lender protections (Martin v. Peyton). She can veto but not initiate or bind.
The result is right but the reason is wrong: labels do not control.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Lender, not partner

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ivan owns Spoke & Chain, a struggling bicycle shop. His friend Jade lends him $60,000. Their written "Loan Agreement" says Jade will receive 30% of the shop's profits until she has received $90,000, may inspect the books monthly, and may veto any single purchase over $15,000. Kurt has worked at the shop for years; Ivan agrees to pay him a salary plus a bonus of 10% of profits. Ivan also lets his cousin Lena, a well-known local cyclist, tell suppliers that she is "Ivan's partner in Spoke & Chain." Lena has no ownership interest in the shop.

Is Kurt a partner in Spoke & Chain?
o: Yes, because he shares in the profits of the business.
No, because profits received as wages raise no presumption of partnership.
Yes, as a partner by estoppel, because he works there openly.
Yes, because he has worked at the shop for years.
A and C.
oe: Profits received as wages do not raise the presumption.
Correct. RUPA § 202(c)(3)(ii); compare Fenwick.
Nothing suggests Kurt was represented to anyone as a partner.
Length of service does not create a partnership.
Neither is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Profit share as wages

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ivan owns Spoke & Chain, a struggling bicycle shop. His friend Jade lends him $60,000. Their written "Loan Agreement" says Jade will receive 30% of the shop's profits until she has received $90,000, may inspect the books monthly, and may veto any single purchase over $15,000. Kurt has worked at the shop for years; Ivan agrees to pay him a salary plus a bonus of 10% of profits. Ivan also lets his cousin Lena, a well-known local cyclist, tell suppliers that she is "Ivan's partner in Spoke & Chain." Lena has no ownership interest in the shop.

Rimco, a parts supplier, relies on Lena's statement that she is Ivan's partner and sells the shop $8,000 of parts on credit. The shop cannot pay. Which of the following statements best describes Lena's liability?
o: Lena is not liable, because there was no partnership in fact between them.
Lena is liable to all of the shop's creditors, whether or not they relied on her statement.
Lena is liable only if she actually shared in the shop's profits.
Lena is liable to Rimco as a purported partner, because Rimco relied on her statement.
None of the above.
oe: Partnership by estoppel exists precisely when there is no partnership in fact.
Liability runs only to those who relied on the representation, though a public representation reaches anyone who relies on it.
Profit sharing is irrelevant to purported-partner liability.
Correct. RUPA § 308 (UPA § 16): a person who represents herself as a partner is liable to one who relies on the representation in entering a transaction (Young v. Jones).
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Partnership by estoppel

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ivan owns Spoke & Chain, a struggling bicycle shop. His friend Jade lends him $60,000. Their written "Loan Agreement" says Jade will receive 30% of the shop's profits until she has received $90,000, may inspect the books monthly, and may veto any single purchase over $15,000. Kurt has worked at the shop for years; Ivan agrees to pay him a salary plus a bonus of 10% of profits. Ivan also lets his cousin Lena, a well-known local cyclist, tell suppliers that she is "Ivan's partner in Spoke & Chain." Lena has no ownership interest in the shop.

Suppose Jade's agreement also lets her decide which bicycles the shop stocks, requires her approval of all hiring, gives her an option to take over the shop, and puts Ivan's signed resignation in escrow, and Jade begins negotiating deals with suppliers in the shop's name. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Jade is now more likely a co-owner, since enough control terms together can cross the line.
Jade is still a lender, because each term alone is a reasonable protection for a lender.
Jade can't be a partner, because she does not share in the shop's losses.
Jade becomes Ivan's employee, because she now directs the business.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Martin v. Peyton recognized that enough control terms together can cross the line; it is a question of degree. Initiating deals and directing operations move Jade from protecting a loan toward running the business (compare Cargill and Kaufman-Brown).
Martin v. Peyton evaluated the terms together and warned that enough of them could make a partnership.
Loss sharing is a factor, not a requirement; a partnership can exist without an agreement to share losses.
Nothing suggests employment.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — A question of degree

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ivan owns Spoke & Chain, a struggling bicycle shop. His friend Jade lends him $60,000. Their written "Loan Agreement" says Jade will receive 30% of the shop's profits until she has received $90,000, may inspect the books monthly, and may veto any single purchase over $15,000. Kurt has worked at the shop for years; Ivan agrees to pay him a salary plus a bonus of 10% of profits. Ivan also lets his cousin Lena, a well-known local cyclist, tell suppliers that she is "Ivan's partner in Spoke & Chain." Lena has no ownership interest in the shop.

Assume a court finds Ivan and Jade are partners under the RUPA. A creditor obtains a $50,000 judgment against the partnership, but partnership assets cover only $20,000. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The creditor generally must exhaust partnership assets before reaching the partners' personal assets.
Ivan and Jade are jointly and severally liable for the shortfall.
Jade's liability is capped at the $60,000 she contributed.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. This is the exhaustion rule (RUPA § 307).
True. Partners are jointly and severally liable for all partnership obligations (RUPA § 306(a)).
False. A general partner's liability is unlimited.
Correct. The creditor first exhausts partnership assets, then may pursue either partner for the full shortfall.
C is wrong.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Exhaustion and joint liability

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: FreshCart, a grocery delivery company, employs Mo as a delivery driver. Mo drives a FreshCart van, wears a FreshCart uniform, follows routes FreshCart assigns, and is paid by the hour. FreshCart's written rules forbid drivers to carry passengers or to use the vans for personal errands.

Between two deliveries, Mo drives two blocks off his route to buy coffee and, while doing so, negligently rear-ends Nora's car. Is FreshCart liable to Nora?
o: No, because any departure from the assigned route ends the scope of employment.
Likely not, because at that moment Mo was serving only his own purposes.
Yes, because a minor detour stays within the scope of employment.
Yes, but only if FreshCart was negligent in hiring or training Mo.
None of the above.
oe: Minor deviations (detours) remain within scope; only a substantial departure (a frolic) breaks it.
A brief coffee stop during a delivery shift is a minor deviation incidental to the work.
Correct. Under R2d §§ 228–229, a small, foreseeable deviation is a detour, not a frolic. It remains substantially within the authorized time and space, so FreshCart is vicariously liable.
Respondeat superior is strict liability; no fault is needed.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Detour vs. frolic

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: FreshCart, a grocery delivery company, employs Mo as a delivery driver. Mo drives a FreshCart van, wears a FreshCart uniform, follows routes FreshCart assigns, and is paid by the hour. FreshCart's written rules forbid drivers to carry passengers or to use the vans for personal errands.

Against FreshCart's rules, Mo picks up a hitchhiker who pays him $20 for a ride, and then crashes, injuring the hitchhiker. Applying the reasoning of Brill v. Davajon, which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: FreshCart is liable, because forbidden acts are always within the scope of employment.
FreshCart is likely not liable, because the paid ride served only Mo's purposes.
FreshCart is likely liable, because every risk created by a delivery business is characteristic of it.
Mo is not liable, because he was acting as FreshCart's employee.
None of the above.
oe: Forbidden acts can be within scope, but not always; the purpose prong still matters.

Correct. Carrying a paying passenger for Mo's own $20 was not actuated by any purpose to serve FreshCart. In Brill, a cab driver who pushed a stalled car for $1 against company rules acted outside the scope of employment.
Bushey's enterprise-risk theory is an alternative, but under Brill the personal side deal breaks scope.
An agent is always liable for his own torts (R3d § 7.01).
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Brill v. Davajon

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: FreshCart, a grocery delivery company, employs Mo as a delivery driver. Mo drives a FreshCart van, wears a FreshCart uniform, follows routes FreshCart assigns, and is paid by the hour. FreshCart's written rules forbid drivers to carry passengers or to use the vans for personal errands.

While Mo unloads groceries at a customer's house, the customer insults him and repeatedly grabs at the bags, keeping him from finishing the delivery. Mo shoves the customer, who falls and is injured. Under Manning v. Grimsley, which of the following statements is true?
o: FreshCart may be liable, because force used against someone interfering with the job can be within scope.
FreshCart cannot be liable, because intentional torts are never within the scope of an employee's job.
FreshCart is liable only if it later ratified Mo's shove.
FreshCart is liable only if Mo was an independent contractor, not an employee.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. An employee's assault in response to the plaintiff's conduct that presently interferes with his ability to do his job can be within the scope of employment. In Manning the pitcher threw at hecklers who were interfering with his warm-up; the battery claim went to the jury.
Intentional torts can be within scope (R2d § 228(1)(d)).
Ratification is one route, but scope of employment is enough.
Respondeat superior applies to employees, not independent contractors.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Manning v. Grimsley

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: FreshCart, a grocery delivery company, employs Mo as a delivery driver. Mo drives a FreshCart van, wears a FreshCart uniform, follows routes FreshCart assigns, and is paid by the hour. FreshCart's written rules forbid drivers to carry passengers or to use the vans for personal errands.

Suppose FreshCart's contract calls Mo an "independent contractor," but FreshCart still assigns his routes, sets his hours, requires the uniform, supplies the van, and can fire him at will. Which of the following statements is true?
o: FreshCart's right to control Mo's work, not whether it actually exercises that control, is what matters.
The contract label is informative but not dispositive.
Because the contract calls Mo an independent contractor, FreshCart cannot be vicariously liable for his torts.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The test is the right to control the manner and means of the work.
True. Labels and disclaimers do not decide employee status (Humble Oil).
False. The label yields to the actual relationship.
Correct. With this much control, Mo is likely an employee despite the label.
C is wrong.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Employee vs. independent contractor

q: Under the UPA (1914), which of the following is true of a partner's power to dissolve a partnership for a definite term before the term ends?
o: The partner has neither the power nor the right to dissolve before the term ends.
The partner has the power to dissolve, but using it early is wrongful.
The partnership agreement can eliminate the partner's power to dissolve.
The partner has the right to dissolve whenever the partnership is losing money.
None of the above.
oe: Under the UPA a partner always has the power to dissolve.
Correct. Power, not always the right: premature dissolution is wrongful but still occurs (Collins v. Lewis).
The power cannot be contracted away.
Losses alone do not give a right to dissolve, especially losses caused by the partner (Collins).
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Power vs. right (UPA)

q: Under the RUPA (1997), a filed statement of partnership authority that LIMITS a partner's authority:
o: Is constructive notice of the limit to every third party.
Is void, because partners can't limit each other's authority by filing.
Generally doesn't bind third parties without knowledge, except real property limits.
Binds only banks and other institutional lenders that extend credit.
None of the above.
oe: Filed limits are generally not notice to third parties.
Statements are valid; a filed grant of authority is conclusive for those who give value in reliance.
Correct. RUPA § 303: filed limits are not notice to third parties, except properly recorded limits on authority to transfer the partnership's real property.
No special rule applies to lenders.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Statement of partnership authority

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the duties an agent owes to the principal?
o: The duty of care.
The duty of obedience to instructions.
The duty of loyalty.
The duty of disclosure.
The duty of indemnification.
oe: An agent's duty (R3d § 8.08).
An agent's duty (R3d § 8.09).
An agent's duty (R3d § 8.01).
An agent's duty (R3d § 8.11).

Correct: this is NOT an agent's duty. Indemnifying the other party for losses suffered in carrying out instructions is the PRINCIPAL's duty to the agent, and the principal's duties are contractual, not fiduciary (R3d §§ 8.14–8.15).
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Agent's duties

q: Which of the following statements about capacity in agency is true?
o: The principal needs full capacity; the agent needs only minimal capacity.
The agent must have full contractual capacity, just like the principal does.
A minor can't act as an agent, because a minor lacks capacity.
A minor's appointment of an agent is void from the start.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. R3d §§ 3.04–3.05. The agent's acts are the principal's, so only the principal needs full capacity.
An agent needs only minimal capacity.
A minor may be an agent.
It is voidable, not void.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Capacity

q: Under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001), which of the following are rights of a limited partner?
o: To share in the profits of the limited partnership.
To inspect and copy required information and records of the limited partnership.
To bind the limited partnership on ordinary business matters.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Both general and limited partners own the firm and share profits.
True. Limited partners have information rights.
False. A limited partner has no right or power, as a limited partner, to act for or bind the LP.
Correct. Limited partners share profits and have information rights but cannot bind the firm.
C is wrong.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Limited partners' rights

q: Under UPA § 40(b), in what order are the liabilities of a partnership paid on liquidation?
o: Partners' capital, partners' loans, outside creditors, partners' profits.
Outside creditors, partners' loans, partners' capital, partners' profits.
Outside creditors, partners' capital, partners' loans, partners' profits.
Partners' loans, outside creditors, partners' capital, partners' profits.
None of the above.
oe: Outside creditors are always paid first.
Correct. That is the UPA § 40(b) order. (RUPA instead pays all creditors, including partner-creditors, together, then contributions, then surplus.)
Under the UPA, partner loans come before capital.
Outside creditors come first.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — UPA § 40(b) order

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn is the general manager of Atlas Signs, Inc. She works at will and has no non-compete agreement. Atlas spent two years and substantial money building a confidential customer database listing each client's pricing and renewal dates; access is password-protected. While still employed, Quinn decides to start her own sign company.

Which of the following may Quinn do while still employed by Atlas without breaching her fiduciary duties?
o: Form an LLC for her new business and lease office space.
Arrange financing for the new business.
Recruit Atlas's key designers to join her new company before she resigns.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Permitted. Preparing to compete is allowed if not otherwise wrongful (R3d § 8.04).
Permitted preparation.
Not permitted. Using her position to raid the principal's staff while still employed is a breach (Bancroft-Whitney).
Correct. Forming the entity, leasing space, and lining up financing are permitted preparation; soliciting co-workers during the agency is not.
C is a breach.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Preparing to compete

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn is the general manager of Atlas Signs, Inc. She works at will and has no non-compete agreement. Atlas spent two years and substantial money building a confidential customer database listing each client's pricing and renewal dates; access is password-protected. While still employed, Quinn decides to start her own sign company.

Before she leaves, a large hospital asks Quinn for a bid on 50 signs. Believing Atlas lacks the capacity to fill the order, Quinn refers the hospital to a friend's shop in exchange for a 10% kickback, without telling Atlas. Applying General Automotive Manufacturing Co. v. Singer, which of the following statements is true?
o: There is no breach, because Atlas could not have filled the order anyway.
Quinn breached her duty of loyalty and must disgorge the kickback.
Quinn is liable only if Atlas proves it lost profits on the order.
Quinn breached only the duty of care, by misjudging Atlas's capacity.
None of the above.
oe: The agent may not decide for herself which opportunities belong to the principal.
Correct. Quinn had to disclose the opportunity and let Atlas decide. In Singer, the manager who secretly sent orders elsewhere and kept the markup had to disgorge his profits.
The remedy for a secret profit is disgorgement; no loss is needed (Reading).
A secret kickback is a loyalty breach.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Diverting an opportunity

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn is the general manager of Atlas Signs, Inc. She works at will and has no non-compete agreement. Atlas spent two years and substantial money building a confidential customer database listing each client's pricing and renewal dates; access is password-protected. While still employed, Quinn decides to start her own sign company.

After resigning, Quinn uses a printout of Atlas's customer database to solicit Atlas's customers. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Atlas may enjoin Quinn's use of the list, since it is confidential.
Quinn may use the list freely, because her duties ended when she resigned.
Quinn may use the list, because she never signed a non-compete agreement.
Atlas can recover only if Quinn signed a confidentiality agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A former agent may compete but may not use trade secrets, written lists, or confidential information after the agency ends (R3d § 8.05; Town & Country).
The duty not to use the principal's confidential information survives termination.
A non-compete is not needed to protect confidential information.
The fiduciary duty protects confidential information without a contract.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Confidential customer list

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn is the general manager of Atlas Signs, Inc. She works at will and has no non-compete agreement. Atlas spent two years and substantial money building a confidential customer database listing each client's pricing and renewal dates; access is password-protected. While still employed, Quinn decides to start her own sign company.

Suppose instead that Atlas's customer list was widely known in the industry, sign buyers routinely shop around, and Atlas took no steps to keep the list secret. Under Corroon & Black-Rutters & Roberts, Inc. v. Hosch, which of the following statements is true?
o: Quinn is still liable, because every customer list is a trade secret.
Quinn is likely not liable, because the list is not a trade secret.
Quinn is liable only if she solicits within one year of leaving.
Quinn is liable because she was a general manager with access to it.
None of the above.
oe: Customer lists are trade secrets only when the Restatement secrecy factors favor protection.

Correct. Without a non-compete, a departing agent may solicit former clients. In Corroon, widely accessible lists in a market where buyers shop around were not trade secrets (contrast Town & Country).
No such time rule applies without a non-compete.
Her rank does not make a public list secret.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Corroon & Black v. Hosch

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Quinn is the general manager of Atlas Signs, Inc. She works at will and has no non-compete agreement. Atlas spent two years and substantial money building a confidential customer database listing each client's pricing and renewal dates; access is password-protected. o: Disgorgement of Quinn's profits from the breach.
Withholding Quinn's compensation for the period of her intentional breach.
An injunction, and a claim against a competitor that knowingly cooperated in the breach.

A, B and C.
oe: Available.
Available.
Available. In Bancroft-Whitney, the competitor was liable too.

Pat is dissociated and is bought out, while the partnership continues without dissolution.
Pat's announcement dissolves the partnership, but wrongfully.
The partnership dissolves rightfully, because any partner may dissolve at any time.
None of the above.

They may continue, paying Pat his interest less damages and without goodwill.
They may continue but must pay Pat the full value of his interest, including goodwill.
They may expel Pat and continue without paying him anything.
None of the above.

Goodwill is excluded and damages are deducted.
Pat is still entitled to the value of his interest, less damages.
B is correct.

If Rae and Sid continue the business, may they keep using the boat-lift design Pat contributed?
o: Yes. In Pav-Saver, the innocent partner kept using the wrongdoer's patents.
No, because contributed intellectual property reverts to the contributor on dissolution.
Only if the partnership agreement expressly gives them that right.
Only if they pay Pat a full market royalty for the design.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In Pav-Saver Corp. v. Vasso Corp., the innocent partner could continue the business and keep using the patents the wrongdoer contributed, valuing the wrongdoer's interest without goodwill. Plan in advance for what happens to contributed property.

No royalty was required; damages and the exclusion of goodwill reduce what Pat receives.

o: The partnership dissolves.
The dissolution is not wrongful.
Pat's estate becomes a partner in Pat's place.

Whether the physicians owned shares of the corporation.
The common-law element of control, applied through the EEOC's factors.
Whether the physicians received fixed salaries rather than profits.
None of the above.
oe: Titles do not control.
Ownership alone does not decide employee status.

Correct. Control is applied through the EEOC's six factors, such as whether the organization can hire, fire, and supervise the person and whether the person shares in profits, losses, and liabilities. Owners who run the business are employers, not employees; the case was remanded.
Salary is not the test.

It is not otherwise reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the partnership agreement.

A § 801 ground.
A § 801 ground.

The principal negligently selected an incompetent contractor.

The third party knew the agent lacked authority.
A and C.
A, B and C.

Nabisco never actually received Stroud's notice.
Buying bread was outside a grocery's ordinary course.
None of the above.

Correct. Buying bread was ordinary business, and with two equal partners Stroud "was not, and could not be, a majority."

It was squarely within the ordinary course.

Shielding the firm's assets from the owners' personal creditors.
Separating partners' capital accounts from their profits.
Requiring creditors to exhaust partnership assets first.

Tara is dissociated, and her early withdrawal is wrongful.
The partnership automatically dissolves on her withdrawal.
Tara is not dissociated until the other partners consent.
None of the above.
oe: A partner always has the power to dissociate by express will (§ 602(a)).
Correct. § 602(b): in a term partnership, withdrawing by express will before the term ends is wrongful.
Under RUPA, dissociation does not necessarily dissolve a term partnership.
No consent is needed.

In March 2027, Tara gives written notice that she is withdrawing immediately to take a job with a competitor.

Must Pine Ridge be wound up?
o: Yes. A partner's dissociation from a term partnership automatically dissolves it.
Yes, if Tara demands it as part of her withdrawal notice.
No. It continues unless half the remaining partners vote within 90 days to wind up.
No. Only a court may dissolve a partnership for a term.
None of the above.
oe: Dissociation leads to dissolution only in the circumstances § 801 lists.
A wrongfully dissociating partner cannot force winding up.
Correct. § 801(2): it continues unless, within 90 days after a wrongful or death-type dissociation, at least half of the remaining partners (here, either Uma or Wes) express their will to wind it up.
The remaining partners may choose to wind up within 90 days.

Their written agreement states that the partnership will continue until December 31, 2030. The agreement has no buyout or expulsion provisions. In March 2027, Tara gives written notice that she is withdrawing immediately to take a job with a competitor.

If Uma and Wes continue the business, how is the price for Tara's interest determined?
o: Liquidation value only, because Tara's dissociation was wrongful.
Book value as shown in Tara's capital account on the firm's books.
Going-concern value, excluding goodwill.
The greater of liquidation or going-concern value, less damages, plus interest.
None of the above.
oe: The price uses the greater of liquidation or going-concern value.
Book value applies only if the agreement says so (as in G & S v. Belman).
Excluding goodwill is the UPA § 38 rule for wrongful dissolvers; RUPA has no goodwill deduction.

Correct. RUPA § 701: the amount distributable to Tara if the assets were sold at the greater of liquidation value or going-concern value without her, minus damages for her wrongful dissociation, plus interest.

In March 2027, Tara gives written notice that she is withdrawing immediately to take a job with a competitor.

When is Tara entitled to be paid?
o: Within 120 days after her written demand, as with any dissociated partner.
Not until 2030, unless earlier payment won't cause undue hardship.
Never, because she dissociated wrongfully before the term ended.
Immediately on dissociation, with interest from that date.
None of the above.
oe: That is the general rule, but not for a wrongful dissociator from a term partnership.
Correct. A partner who wrongfully dissociates before the term ends must wait until the term expires, unless she shows earlier payment will not cause undue hardship (with security and interest).
A wrongful dissociator is still bought out, less damages.
There is no immediate payment right.
B is correct.

Two months after leaving, Tara signs a contract in Pine Ridge's name for a large landscaping job with Xeno Corp., a longtime customer that does not know she has left. No statement of dissociation has been filed. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership may be bound, because for two years a dissociated partner's act binds the partnership if the other party reasonably believed she was still a partner and had no notice of her dissociation.
Tara is liable to the partnership for any loss caused by the obligation.
The partnership can never be bound by a dissociated partner.
A and B.
None of the above.
oe: True (§ 702). Filing a statement of dissociation would cut this off after 90 days (§ 704).
True. A dissociated partner who binds the firm this way must answer for the loss (§ 702(b)).
False. Apparent authority lingers for up to two years.
Correct.

Q12–15 HYPO: BurgerBarn, Inc. franchises fast-food restaurants. An employee of Yolanda's with a record of violence, hired without a background check, assaults a customer in the parking lot. The customer sues BurgerBarn for negligent hiring and supervision. Under Kerl v. Rasmussen, which of the following statements is true?
o: BurgerBarn is liable, because it controls the trademarks, recipes, and uniforms.
BurgerBarn is not liable, because it did not control Yolanda's hiring or supervision.
BurgerBarn is liable, because franchisors are strictly liable for franchisees' torts.
BurgerBarn is liable, because its periodic quality inspections show control.
None of the above.
oe: Control over brand standards is not control over hiring and supervision.

Correct. Under the majority franchise test from Kerl, a franchisor is vicariously liable only if it controls or has the right to control the daily operation of the specific aspect of the business that caused the harm. Yolanda alone controlled hiring and supervision.
No such rule exists.
Quality and trademark standards are not control.
B is correct.

BurgerBarn cannot be liable, because Yolanda runs an independent business.
A and B.

True.
False. Miller sent both theories to the jury.
Correct. Miller shows both routes to franchisor tort liability.
A and B are true.

Lamkin v. Brooks.

Retained control is one exception, but not the only one.

The ratification is effective if made within a reasonable time.
The seller is bound by estoppel, because Yara relied on the deal.

Q12–15 HYPO: Ada and Ben form a partnership to renovate and resell houses. Ada contributes $50,000 in cash. Ben contributes no money but agrees to do all the renovation work without a salary. They agree to split profits equally but say nothing about losses. After two years, the business is dissolved. After all outside creditors are paid, $20,000 remains.

Applying Kovacik v. Reed, how is the $20,000 distributed?
o: Ada receives the $20,000, and Ben must also pay Ada $15,000.
Ada receives the $20,000, and Ben owes Ada nothing.
Ada and Ben each receive $10,000 under their 50/50 split.
Ben owes Ada $30,000, the full capital loss.
None of the above.
oe: That is the statutory loss-sharing result, which Kovacik rejected.
Correct. Under Kovacik, where one partner contributed only money and the other only services, each loses his own contribution: Ada loses $30,000 of capital and Ben loses his labor.
Capital is returned before anything is split as profit.
Not under any rule.
B is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ada and Ben form a partnership to renovate and resell houses. Ada contributes $50,000 in cash. Ben contributes no money but agrees to do all the renovation work without a salary. They agree to split profits equally but say nothing about losses. After two years, the business is dissolved. After all outside creditors are paid, $20,000 remains.

Applying the statutory default instead (UPA § 18(a), and the rule RUPA follows), how are Ada's and Ben's positions settled?
o: Ada receives the $20,000, and Ben owes her nothing more.
Ben must contribute the full $30,000 capital loss.
Ben must contribute $15,000, so Ada receives $35,000 in all.
Ada and Ben each receive $10,000 of the remaining funds.
None of the above.
oe: That is the Kovacik result.
Losses are shared, not borne entirely by Ben.
Correct. The $30,000 capital loss follows profits (50/50), so each bears $15,000. Ada gets the $20,000 plus Ben's $15,000 contribution.
Capital is returned first.
C is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ada and Ben form a partnership to renovate and resell houses. Ada contributes $50,000 in cash. Ben contributes no money but agrees to do all the renovation work without a salary. They agree to split profits equally but say nothing about losses. After two years, the business is dissolved. After all outside creditors are paid, $20,000 remains.

Which of the following facts would make a court LESS likely to apply the Kovacik rule?
o: Ben was paid a salary for his work.
Ben contributed $500 worth of his own tools as capital.
The agreement said nothing about losses.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Kovacik is not applied when the service partner was paid a salary.
True. Kovacik is not applied when the service partner made any capital contribution, even a nominal one.
False. Silence on losses is the setting where Kovacik applies.
Correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Ada and Ben form a partnership to renovate and resell houses. Ada contributes $50,000 in cash. Ben contributes no money but agrees to do all the renovation work without a salary. They agree to split profits equally but say nothing about losses. After two years, the business is dissolved. After all outside creditors are paid, $20,000 remains.

Suppose instead that Ada and Ben had agreed that "losses shall be shared equally," and an outside creditor still holds an unpaid $10,000 judgment after the partnership's assets are exhausted. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Only Ada is liable to the creditor, because she contributed the capital.
Each is personally liable for the full $10,000, sharing the loss equally between them.
Ben is liable only up to the value of the services he contributed.
Neither partner is liable, because the judgment was against the partnership itself.
None of the above.
oe: Liability to outsiders does not depend on who contributed capital.
Correct. Partners are jointly and severally liable to creditors (RUPA § 306(a)); their agreement governs how they share the loss internally.
A general partner's liability is not capped by his contribution.
After exhaustion, the creditor may pursue the partners personally.
B is correct.
