q: Meinhard v. Salmon is best known for holding that:
o: Co-venturers owe "the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive," including disclosure.
Co-venturers owe no duties once the venture's term is about to expire.
A managing co-venturer may take a renewal lease for himself if he pays a fair price.
A joint venture must be in writing to create fiduciary duties.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A managing co-venturer must at least disclose an opportunity that grows out of the venture. Meinhard received half of the new lease. This is the root of the partnership-opportunity rule.
That was the dissent's view.
Paying a fair price does not cure the failure to disclose.
No writing was required.
A is correct.

q: Which of the following best describes how the RUPA (1997) differs from the UPA (1914) when a partner leaves?
o: Under the RUPA, a partner's departure always dissolves the partnership.
Under the RUPA, a departure is a dissociation leading to either a buyout or winding up.
Under the UPA, a partner's departure is only a dissociation and never a dissolution.
Neither act allows the business to continue after a partner leaves.
None of the above.
oe: That is the UPA rule.
Correct. This is the § 603 "switch": a dissociation leads either to a buyout and continuation under Article 7 or to dissolution and winding up under Article 8.
Under the UPA any partner's departure dissolves the partnership.
Both allow continuation: the UPA through a new firm, and the RUPA through a buyout.
B is correct.

q: In Lind v. Schenley Industries, the company was bound by Kaufman's promise of a 1% commission because:
o: Kaufman had express actual authority to set his subordinates' salaries.
Lind's belief rested on Kaufman's own statements about the scope of his authority.
The company held Kaufman out as its spokesman on salary, giving him apparent authority.
The company's president later ratified Kaufman's promise to Lind.
None of the above.
oe: Only the president could set pay; Kaufman had no actual authority.
The agent's own say-so cannot create apparent authority.

Correct. By sending Lind to Kaufman about salary and making Kaufman his superior, the company held Kaufman out as its spokesman. Apparent authority comes from the principal's manifestations, including the position it gave the agent.
There was no ratification.
C is correct.

q: Under the ULLCA, in a manager-managed LLC, which of the following requires the consent of all members?
o: An act outside the ordinary course of the LLC's activities.
Amending the operating agreement.
An ordinary hiring decision.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True.
True.
False. Ordinary matters are decided by the managers.
Correct. As in a member-managed LLC, acts outside the ordinary course and amendments to the operating agreement need unanimous member consent.
C is wrong.

q: In Ira S. Bushey & Sons, Inc. v. United States, Judge Friendly held the government liable for the drunk sailor's flooding of the drydock primarily because:
o: An enterprise must bear risks "characteristic of its activities," like sailors' drinking.
The sailor acted at least partly with a purpose to serve his employer.
The government ratified the sailor's conduct by failing to discipline him at all afterward.
The government negligently supervised the sailor while he was on leave.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. This is the enterprise-risk alternative to the R2d motive test.
Friendly accepted that the sailor had no purpose to serve the employer.
There was no ratification.
The case rests on vicarious, not direct, liability.
A is correct.

q: Which of the following is NOT an event of dissociation under RUPA § 601?
o: The partner's filing of a voluntary bankruptcy petition.
The partner's death.
The partner's expulsion by judicial order for misconduct.
The partner's notice of express will to withdraw from the firm.
A creditor obtains a charging order against the partner's interest.
oe: A § 601 event.
A § 601 event.
A § 601 event.
A § 601 event.
Correct: NOT dissociation. A charging order is only a lien on distributions from the partner's transferable interest. Neither a charging order nor a transfer of an interest dissociates the partner.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kim, Lou, and Mia are partners in KLM Realty, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that buys, renovates, and leases small apartment buildings in Dover. Lou manages acquisitions. The partnership agreement says nothing about fiduciary duties or competition, and it has no fixed term.

A broker who knows Lou through his work for KLM offers Lou a six-unit building in Dover at a bargain price. Lou buys it with his own money without telling Kim or Mia. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Lou committed no breach, because he bought it with his own money.
Lou breached only the duty of care, by failing to consult his partners.
Lou breached his duty of loyalty by taking a partnership opportunity.
Lou committed no breach, because pursuing his own interest is not itself a breach.
None of the above.
oe: Using his own money does not matter; the opportunity belonged to the partnership.
This is a loyalty problem.

Correct. RUPA § 409(b)(1); the organizational opportunity doctrine (Meinhard). The opportunity came to him through his partnership role and fits KLM's business, so he must hold the building, or his profit from it, for the partnership.
Section 409(e) does not excuse taking a partnership opportunity.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Appropriating an opportunity

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kim, Lou, and Mia are partners in KLM Realty, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that buys, renovates, and leases small apartment buildings in Dover. Lou manages acquisitions. The partnership agreement says nothing about fiduciary duties or competition, and it has no fixed term.

Lou sells KLM a building he personally owns, at full fair market value, after disclosing all material facts, and Kim and Mia approve the sale. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Lou breached his duty of loyalty, because a partner may never deal adversely with the firm.
Lou committed no breach, because his partners authorized it after full disclosure.
Lou breached his duty unless a court later approves the sale.
Lou breached his duty unless the price was below fair market value.
None of the above.
oe: Adverse dealing can be authorized after full disclosure.
Correct. RUPA § 409(f) (authorization or ratification after full disclosure) and § 409(g) (fairness is also a defense to self-dealing).
Court approval is not required.
A fair price, plus disclosure and consent, is enough.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Authorized self-dealing

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kim, Lou, and Mia are partners in KLM Realty, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that buys, renovates, and leases small apartment buildings in Dover. Lou manages acquisitions. The partnership agreement says nothing about fiduciary duties or competition, and it has no fixed term.

Mia forgets to renew the partnership's fire-insurance policy. A fire then causes an uninsured loss. Her lapse was ordinary negligence, not gross negligence. Is Mia liable to the partnership for breach of the duty of care?
o: Yes, because any negligence in managing the business breaches the duty of care.
Yes, because partners are strictly liable for partnership losses they cause.
No, because partners owe one another no duty of care at all.
No, because her lapse was not grossly negligent, reckless, or intentional.
None of the above.
oe: Ordinary negligence is not a breach under RUPA.
There is no strict liability.
Partners do owe a duty of care, but a limited one.
Correct. RUPA § 409(c): a partner's duty of care is limited to refraining from gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Ordinary negligence

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kim, Lou, and Mia are partners in KLM Realty, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that buys, renovates, and leases small apartment buildings in Dover. Lou manages acquisitions. The partnership agreement says nothing about fiduciary duties or competition, and it has no fixed term.

Ned, a retired KLM partner, receives a pension that depends on KLM's success. Kim and Lou negligently approve a merger that causes KLM to collapse, and Ned's pension stops. Ned sues them. Under Bane v. Ferguson, which of the following statements is true?
o: Ned wins, because partners owe fiduciary duties to retired partners.
Ned loses, because partners owe their duties to current partners only.
Ned wins only if the decision was a merger rather than an ordinary act.
Ned wins because he is a third-party beneficiary of the partnership agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Bane held the opposite.

Correct. Partners owe their duties to current partners, not former ones, and the business judgment rule would shield mere negligence anyway. Bane shows who is owed partner duties and how low the duty of care is.
The type of decision does not matter.
The court rejected his claims.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Bane v. Ferguson

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Kim, Lou, and Mia are partners in KLM Realty, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997) that buys, renovates, and leases small apartment buildings in Dover. Lou manages acquisitions. The partnership agreement says nothing about fiduciary duties or competition, and it has no fixed term.

Kim and Lou decide to dissolve KLM so they can keep running its profitable business without Mia. They lock Mia out, form a new LLC, and transfer KLM's leases to it. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Kim and Lou may dissolve the at-will partnership, but they must do so in good faith.
Their fiduciary duties continue through winding up, so they must account to Mia for partnership property and opportunities.
Fiduciary duties end at dissolution, so the transfer is proper.
None of the above.
A and B.
oe: True. Page v. Page: at-will partners may dissolve, but not to freeze out a partner and grab the business.
True. Second Measure, Inc. v. Kim; Monin.
False. Duties continue until winding up is complete.
A and B are true.
Correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Freeze-out on dissolution

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Opal, Pete, and Quincy form Riverbend Outfitters, LLC, a kayak-rental business, under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). The certificate of organization is properly filed. Their operating agreement says nothing about management, distributions, or withdrawal.

Who manages Riverbend, and how are ordinary decisions made?
o: It is member-managed, and ordinary matters are decided by a majority of members.
Riverbend is manager-managed by Opal, as the first member to sign.
Each member votes in proportion to the capital he or she contributed.
All decisions, ordinary or not, require the unanimous consent of all three members.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Member-management is the default; manager-management exists only if the agreement provides for it. Each member has equal rights in management, and ordinary matters are decided by a majority.
Nothing provides for managers.
Equal rights are the default, regardless of contribution.
Only acts outside the ordinary course and amendments to the operating agreement require unanimity.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Default management

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Opal, Pete, and Quincy form Riverbend Outfitters, LLC, a kayak-rental business, under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). The certificate of organization is properly filed. Their operating agreement says nothing about management, distributions, or withdrawal.

Riverbend cannot pay a $40,000 judgment arising from a kayaking accident caused by one of its employees. The plaintiff seeks to hold Opal, Pete, and Quincy personally liable because they never held formal meetings or kept minutes. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The members are personally liable, because they did not observe formalities.
The members are not personally liable merely because they are members.
The members are jointly and severally liable, like general partners.
The members are liable because Riverbend never filed a statement of qualification as an LLP.
None of the above.
oe: Failure to observe formalities is not a ground for liability (§ 304).

Correct. ULLCA § 304: members are not personally liable for the LLC's obligations solely by reason of being members, and failing to observe formalities is not a ground for liability. Veil piercing is the main exception.
LLC members have a full liability shield without filing an LLP statement.
An LLC needs no LLP filing; its certificate of organization gives the shield.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — No liability for status

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Opal, Pete, and Quincy form Riverbend Outfitters, LLC, a kayak-rental business, under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). The certificate of organization is properly filed. Their operating agreement says nothing about management, distributions, or withdrawal.

Riverbend's debts exceed its assets, but Pete and Quincy vote to distribute $30,000 to the members anyway. Opal objects. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The distribution is proper because a majority of the members voted to approve it.
The distribution is improper, but no one is personally liable for it.
All three members are personally liable for the improper distribution.
It is improper, and Pete and Quincy, who consented, are liable for the excess.
None of the above.
oe: A majority vote cannot authorize a distribution that leaves the LLC insolvent.
Members who consented are liable.
Opal objected.
Correct. ULLCA §§ 405–406. The distribution is improper because it would leave the LLC insolvent, and the members who consented to it are personally liable for the excess.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Improper distribution

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Opal, Pete, and Quincy form Riverbend Outfitters, LLC, a kayak-rental business, under a statute based on the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA). The certificate of organization is properly filed. Their operating agreement says nothing about management, distributions, or withdrawal.

Quincy withdraws from Riverbend. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Quincy may make Riverbend buy his interest at fair value.
Riverbend must dissolve and wind up its business.
No buyout; Quincy keeps his economic interest only as a transferee.
Quincy keeps his management rights.
None of the above.
oe: The ULLCA has no mandatory buyout.
A member's dissociation does not dissolve the LLC.
Correct. ULLCA §§ 601–603. This is a key contrast with RUPA § 701.
A dissociated member loses management rights.
C is correct.

q: Martin v. Peyton held that the wealthy lenders were not partners of the brokerage firm primarily because:
o: They did not share in the firm's profits, only in a fixed return.
Their information and veto rights were reasonable protections for a large, risky loan.
They had no knowledge of the firm's business or its finances.
Their agreement expressly said they were not partners, and the court found that controlling.
None of the above.
oe: They did receive 40% of profits (capped), but as compensation for the loan.

Correct. Their information rights, veto over speculative deals, option to buy in, and escrowed resignations protected a large, risky loan; they could veto but not initiate transactions or bind the firm. Whether lenders cross into partnership is "a question of degree."
They had extensive information rights.
Labels do not control; the court examined the substance.
B is correct.

q: Which of the following correctly states the rule of estoppel under Restatement (Third) of Agency § 2.05?
o: A principal is bound to a contract whenever a third party reasonably believes an agent is authorized to act.
Estoppel binds the third party to the contract as well as the principal, like ratification.
One who carelessly caused, or failed to correct, the belief is liable to a third party who detrimentally relied.
Estoppel requires that the principal know of the specific transaction in advance of it.
None of the above.
oe: That overstates even apparent authority, which requires a manifestation by the principal.
Estoppel protects the relying third party; it does not bind that third party.

Correct. That is the § 2.05 rule (R2d § 8B): a person who intentionally or carelessly caused the belief that a transaction was on its account, or who knew of the belief and failed to take reasonable steps to correct it, is liable to a third party justifiably induced to make a detrimental change in position.
Careless conduct is enough; advance knowledge is not required.
C is correct.

q: Under the RUPA (1997), a transferee of a partner's transferable interest is entitled to:
o: Receive the distributions the transferor would otherwise receive.
Participate in the management of the partnership's business.
Inspect the partnership's books and records on demand.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Correct. A transferee gets distributions only, not management or information rights.
Management rights stay with the partner.
A transferee has no information rights.
B is wrong.
B and C are wrong.

q: Which of the following statements correctly reconciles National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud and Summers v. Dooley?
o: Both cases hold that one of two equal partners can never bind the partnership.
Summers overruled National Biscuit on the authority of equal partners.
Both cases hold that ordinary partnership matters require unanimous consent.
Nabisco governs dealings with outsiders; Summers governs dealings among partners.
None of the above.
oe: In Nabisco, one of two partners did bind the firm to a third party.
They are from different states and address different questions.
Ordinary matters are decided by a majority.

Correct. As to third parties, a partner's ordinary-course act binds the firm despite a co-partner's objection (Nabisco); among the partners, a dissenting half can block reimbursement of an unapproved expense (Summers).
D is correct.

q: Under Restatement (Third) of Agency § 7.07, an employee acts outside the scope of employment when:
o: The employee acts on an independent course of conduct serving no employer purpose.
The employer had expressly forbidden the act in its written work rules.
The employee's act was intentional rather than merely negligent or careless conduct.
The employee was off the employer's premises and outside working hours.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. R3d § 7.07: an employee acts outside scope when engaged in an independent course of conduct not intended to serve any purpose of the employer. The R3d test replaces R2d's time-and-space limits.
Forbidden acts can be within scope.
Intentional torts can be within scope.
Location alone does not decide scope under R3d.
A is correct.

The Texas real estate crash.
Mass financial torts against lawyers and accountants.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Paloma's Furniture runs a large showroom where salespeople wear ordinary clothes and walk the floor helping customers. One afternoon Rafe, a stranger who does not work for Paloma's, stands at the sales desk for an hour. Several employees notice him but do nothing. When Sasha comes in to buy a sofa, Rafe offers to "write up" her order, takes her $900 cash deposit, and disappears.

Sasha sues Paloma's for her $900. Did Rafe have apparent authority to accept the deposit?
o: Yes, because Rafe dressed and acted like a salesperson on the floor.
No, because the appearance came from Rafe, not from Paloma's.
Yes, because Sasha reasonably believed he was a salesperson.
No, because Rafe was not on Paloma's payroll as a salesperson.
None of the above.
oe: Appearances the impostor creates himself do not count.
Correct. Apparent authority must be traceable to the principal's manifestations, not to the impostor's own conduct. Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.: there was no apparent authority.
Reasonable belief is necessary but not sufficient; it must come from the principal.
Pay is irrelevant; Rafe was not an agent at all.
B is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Paloma's Furniture runs a large showroom where salespeople wear ordinary clothes and walk the floor helping customers. One afternoon Rafe, a stranger who does not work for Paloma's, stands at the sales desk for an hour. Several employees notice him but do nothing. When Sasha comes in to buy a sofa, Rafe offers to "write up" her order, takes her $900 cash deposit, and disappears.

What is Sasha's best theory of recovery against Paloma's?
o: Ratification, because Paloma's employees saw Rafe and did nothing.
Inherent agency power, because Rafe stood at the store's sales desk.
Estoppel, if the store's carelessness let Rafe pose as staff and Sasha relied.
Respondeat superior, because the theft happened on Paloma's premises during business hours.
None of the above.
oe: Paloma's never affirmed Rafe's act.
Rafe was not an agent, so there was no agency relationship from which inherent power could arise.

Correct. A store must use reasonable care to keep impostors from posing as its staff, and Paloma's may be liable if its carelessness caused Sasha's reasonable, detrimental reliance. Hoddeson ordered a new trial on this theory.
Rafe was not an employee.
C is correct.

Her reliance on that appearance was reasonable.
She changed her position to her detriment by paying the deposit.

A, B and C.

Required.

Suppose instead that Rafe was a Paloma's salesman who had been fired the day before but was still wearing his Paloma's name tag. Sasha, a repeat customer who had bought from Rafe before, gives him the deposit. Which of the following is the most accurate statement?
o: Paloma's may be bound, because Rafe's apparent authority lingers.
Firing Rafe automatically ended his apparent authority as well.
Paloma's is not liable, because Rafe was no longer its agent.
Rafe is not personally liable, because he purported to act for Paloma's.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Terminating actual authority does not automatically end apparent authority.
Apparent authority can survive termination of actual authority.
His lingering apparent authority can still bind Paloma's.
Rafe is liable for his own fraud and on the implied warranty of authority.
A is correct.

Q7–11 HYPO: Paloma's Furniture runs a large showroom where salespeople wear ordinary clothes and walk the floor helping customers. One afternoon Rafe, a stranger who does not work for Paloma's, stands at the sales desk for an hour. Several employees notice him but do nothing. When Sasha comes in to buy a sofa, Rafe offers to "write up" her order, takes her $900 cash deposit, and disappears.

Suppose instead that Rafe was a current salesman who took Sasha's deposit for a custom order he had no authority to accept. Paloma's learns all the facts, keeps the deposit, and delivers part of the order, but refuses to deliver the rest. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Paloma's ratified only the part of the order it chose to deliver.
There was no ratification, because it wasn't in writing.
There was no ratification, because Rafe lacked authority.
By knowingly keeping the benefits, Paloma's ratified the entire order.
None of the above.
oe: There is no partial ratification.
Ratification may be implied from conduct.
Ratification exists precisely to adopt unauthorized acts.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tess and Uri are partners in T&U Catering, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Tess bought a delivery van with her own savings, titled it in her own name, and lets the partnership use it. Uri bought a commercial mixer with a partnership check and titled it in his own name, with no reference to the partnership. Vance, a personal creditor of Tess's, holds a $25,000 judgment against her.

Who owns the van and the mixer?
o: Both are partnership property, because the partnership uses both.
The van is presumed Tess's; the mixer is presumed partnership property.
Both are the separate property of the partner in whose name they are titled.
The van is partnership property and the mixer belongs to Uri.
None of the above.
oe: Use by the partnership does not make property partnership property.
Correct. RUPA § 204: property in a partner's name without partnership funds is presumed separate even if the firm uses it; property bought with partnership funds is presumed partnership property.
The partnership check makes the mixer presumptively partnership property.
This reverses the presumptions.
B is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tess and Uri are partners in T&U Catering, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Tess bought a delivery van with her own savings, titled it in her own name, and lets the partnership use it. Uri bought a commercial mixer with a partnership check and titled it in his own name, with no reference to the partnership. Vance, a personal creditor of Tess's, holds a $25,000 judgment against her.

What is Vance's remedy against Tess's interest in the partnership?
o: A charging order, a lien on Tess's partnership distributions.
Seizing the mixer or other partnership assets to satisfy the judgment.
Becoming a partner in Tess's place until the debt is paid.
Forcing the partnership to dissolve and pay out Tess's share.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 504.
A partner's personal creditor cannot reach partnership property.
A creditor never becomes a partner without the partners' consent.
A charging order does not by itself dissolve the partnership.
A is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tess and Uri are partners in T&U Catering, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Tess bought a delivery van with her own savings, titled it in her own name, and lets the partnership use it. Vance, a personal creditor of Tess's, holds a $25,000 judgment against her.

Tess transfers her entire transferable interest in the partnership to her sister, Wynn. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Wynn becomes a partner.
Wynn receives only Tess's distributions, with no management or information rights.
Tess remains a partner, but Uri may expel her because she transferred all of her transferable interest.
B and C.
A, B and C.
oe: False. A transferee does not become a partner.
True.
True. A partner who has transferred all of her interest may be expelled by the unanimous vote of the other partners (§ 601(4)).
Correct.
A is wrong.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Tess and Uri are partners in T&U Catering, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Tess bought a delivery van with her own savings, titled it in her own name, and lets the partnership use it. Uri bought a commercial mixer with a partnership check and titled it in his own name, with no reference to the partnership. Vance, a personal creditor of Tess's, holds a $25,000 judgment against her.

In deciding whether property acquired by a partner is partnership property, which consideration matters most under In re Fulton and RUPA § 204?
o: Who actually uses the property day to day.
Whose name appears on the property's insurance policy.
The partners' intent at acquisition, shown by title and the source of funds.
The partnership's tax returns, which are conclusive on ownership.
None of the above.
oe: Use alone does not decide ownership.
Not a recognized test.
Correct. In Fulton the trailer was partnership property based on title, purpose, and intent at acquisition, even though a partner's grandmother lent the money.
Tax returns are evidence, not conclusive.
C is correct.

q: In Singer v. Singer, two partners who bought a parcel the family partnership had discussed buying did not breach their fiduciary duties because:
o: The partnership agreement expressly allowed partners to compete for themselves.
They paid fair value for the parcel and used their own money.
The partnership lacked the funds to buy the parcel at the time.
Meinhard v. Salmon applies only to joint ventures, not to ongoing partnerships.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The clause allowed even "predatory" competition; only taking existing partnership assets or funds would breach. Partners can contract around the opportunity rule.
Fair value was not the basis of the decision.
Not the basis of the decision.
Meinhard's principles apply to partnerships too.
A is correct.

q: Under the RUPA, absent a contrary agreement, which of the following requires the consent of all partners?
o: Amending the partnership agreement.
An act outside the ordinary course of the partnership's business.
Admitting a new partner.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Requires unanimity.
Requires unanimity.
Requires unanimity (§ 402).
Incomplete.
Correct. Ordinary matters are decided by majority, but these three require everyone's consent.

q: In Rose v. Giamatti, the court held that the Commissioner of Baseball was not Major League Baseball's agent for disciplinary purposes because:
o: There was no written agency agreement.
The clubs gave the Commissioner independent authority they could not control.
The Commissioner was not paid by the clubs for his disciplinary work.
Pete Rose had consented to the Commissioner's jurisdiction.
None of the above.
oe: A writing is not required for agency.
Correct. No control, no agency. A person can be an agent for some purposes but not for others.
Pay is irrelevant to agency.
Rose's consent was not the basis of the holding.
B is correct.

o: Tenant in common.
Joint tenant.
Tenant in partnership.
The UPA gives a partner no interest in specific partnership property.
None of the above.
oe: Not the UPA term.
Not the UPA term.
Correct. UPA § 25. RUPA § 501 abolishes it: the partner is not a co-owner of partnership property.
That is the RUPA approach.
C is correct.

o: Sandblasting with proper equipment is not an abnormally dangerous activity.
The contractor's own employees are covered by workers' compensation, which the principal already pays for through the contract price.
Marathon did not know about the inadequate hood.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True.
True. This is Posner's explanation of why the contractor's own workers are treated differently from neighbors.
False. Marathon knew and did nothing.
Correct.
C is false.

q: Which of the following statements about the power and the right to dissociate under RUPA § 602 is true?
o: A partner always has the power to dissociate by express will.
A dissociation can be wrongful only in a partnership for a definite term or undertaking.
A partner who wrongfully dissociates is liable to the partnership and the other partners for the damages caused.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True (§ 602(a); Collins v. Lewis).
False. Breaching an express term of the agreement makes a dissociation wrongful even in an at-will partnership.
Correct.
B is false.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Vera and Walt are equal partners in V&W Print Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Walt writes to Inkwell Supply, the shop's regular supplier: "Do not sell us any more toner on credit; I will not be responsible for it."

Despite Walt's letter, Vera orders $3,000 of toner on credit from Inkwell. Is the partnership bound?
o: No, because Walt's letter told Inkwell that the partnership had withdrawn Vera's authority.
Yes, because buying toner is ordinary business, and Walt alone couldn't restrict Vera.
No, because Inkwell had notice that the two partners disagreed about credit.
Yes, but only Vera is personally liable for the toner bill.
None of the above.
oe: Walt alone could not withdraw Vera's authority over ordinary matters.

Correct. These are the National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud facts. Buying toner is in the ordinary course of business, and Walt, as one of two equal partners, was not a majority and could not restrict Vera's authority.
Notice of a disagreement is not notice that Vera lacked authority.
The partnership, and both partners, are liable.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Two-partner authority

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Vera and Walt are equal partners in V&W Print Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Walt writes to Inkwell Supply, the shop's regular supplier: "Do not sell us any more toner on credit; I will not be responsible for it."

Over Walt's objection, Vera hires a part-time clerk, pays the clerk $2,000 from her own pocket, and asks the partnership to reimburse her. Under Summers v. Dooley, which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership must reimburse Vera, because hiring help is an ordinary business matter.
The partnership must reimburse half the cost, splitting the difference.
Vera gets no reimbursement, because one of two partners is not a majority.
Vera is entitled to reimbursement, because the clerk benefited the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Ordinary matters must be decided by a majority, and Vera had no majority.
No such split exists.
Correct. Business differences must be decided by a majority. Internally, a dissenting half can block the expense.
Benefit does not override the majority rule.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Summers v. Dooley

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Vera and Walt are equal partners in V&W Print Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Walt writes to Inkwell Supply, the shop's regular supplier: "Do not sell us any more toner on credit; I will not be responsible for it."

Vera drives the partnership's truck to drop off a customer's order and, on the way, picks up her son from school. She negligently injures a pedestrian. Under RUPA § 305 and Moren v. Jax Restaurant, which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership is liable, because the errand was still in the ordinary course.
The partnership is liable, but it may recover full indemnity from Vera for the loss.
Only Vera is liable, because she was on a personal errand.
The partnership is liable, but Walt is not personally liable for it.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Moren: a partner's conduct was in the ordinary course of the partnership's business even though it also served a personal purpose.
The statute gives partners indemnity from the partnership, not the reverse (Moren).
The partnership is liable for a partner's wrongful acts in the ordinary course.
Partners are jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Partnership torts (Moren)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Vera and Walt are equal partners in V&W Print Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Walt writes to Inkwell Supply, the shop's regular supplier: "Do not sell us any more toner on credit; I will not be responsible for it."

Without consulting Vera, Walt signs a contract selling the print shop's entire business and building to a competitor. Is the partnership bound?
o: Likely yes, because every partner is an agent of the partnership for its business.
Yes, if the buyer did not know that Vera objected to the sale.
Yes, because Walt signed the contract in the partnership's name.
No, because selling the whole business is outside the ordinary course.
None of the above.
oe: Agency covers only acts apparently in the ordinary course.
The buyer's lack of notice matters only for ordinary-course acts.
Signing in the firm's name does not make an extraordinary act ordinary.
Correct. RUPA § 301(2): an act outside the ordinary course binds the partnership only if the other partners authorized it.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Outside the ordinary course

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Vera and Walt are equal partners in V&W Print Shop, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). They have no written partnership agreement. Walt writes to Inkwell Supply, the shop's regular supplier: "Do not sell us any more toner on credit; I will not be responsible for it."

Vera and Walt sign a written agreement capping any credit purchase at $5,000 without both partners' consent. Which step would MOST effectively protect the partnership against a supplier's later claim on a larger purchase?
o: Nothing more is needed, because suppliers are bound by the partnership agreement.
Nothing more is needed, because third parties have a duty to inquire about a partner's authority.
Notify regular suppliers and lenders of the limit in writing.
Rely on the cap, because any purchase over $5,000 is outside the ordinary course.
None of the above.
oe: Third parties are not bound by private limits they do not know of.
There is no duty to inquire (RNR Investments).

Correct. Under § 301 the partnership escapes liability only if the third party knew or had notice of the lack of authority, so written notice to suppliers and lenders protects it (RNR: notify the lender).
The cap is internal; it does not change what is ordinary business.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Protecting against overreach

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Four accountants, Abe, Bea, Cal, and Dee, plan to practice together. They want to share management equally, avoid entity-level income tax, and avoid personal liability for one another's malpractice.

If the four accountants simply agree to practice together and share profits, without filing anything, what form of business will they have?
o: A limited liability company.
A limited liability partnership.
A general partnership.
A corporation.
A sole proprietorship.
oe: An LLC requires filing.
An LLP requires filing a statement of qualification.
Correct. A general partnership is the default for two or more co-owners; it can be formed without any intent or filing.
A corporation requires filing.
That is the default for one person.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Four accountants, Abe, Bea, Cal, and Dee, plan to practice together. They want to share management equally, avoid entity-level income tax, and avoid personal liability for one another's malpractice.

The accountants file to become a limited liability partnership (LLP). Cal later commits malpractice. Under RUPA § 306(c), which of the following statements is true?
o: Abe, Bea, and Dee are not personally liable for the malpractice obligation solely by reason of being partners.
Cal remains personally liable for his own malpractice.
The partnership's assets may be used to satisfy the claim.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Partnership obligations incurred while an LLP are the LLP's alone.
True. Partners still answer for their own torts.
True. The shield protects partners' personal assets, not the firm's.
Incomplete.
Correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — LLP shield

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Four accountants, Abe, Bea, Cal, and Dee, plan to practice together. They want to share management equally, avoid entity-level income tax, and avoid personal liability for one another's malpractice.

Compared with an LLP, what would an LLC offer the accountants?
o: Limited liability without filing anything with the state, unlike an LLP.
A full liability shield and pass-through taxation, shaped by an operating agreement.
Entity-level income tax only, with no pass-through to members.
Unlimited personal liability for each member, just like partners in a general partnership.
None of the above.
oe: An LLC is formed only by filing a certificate of organization.
Correct. An LLC is formed by filing a certificate of organization, and it is a "creature of contract" that combines limited liability and pass-through taxation. Veil piercing is the main exception.
LLCs are generally pass-through entities.
Members have limited liability.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — LLC alternative

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Four accountants, Abe, Bea, Cal, and Dee, plan to practice together. They want to share management equally, avoid entity-level income tax, and avoid personal liability for one another's malpractice.

Suppose the four never file anything and practice as a general partnership. Dee leaves a year later. A creditor sues on a debt the partnership incurred while Dee was a partner. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Dee remains personally liable for obligations incurred before she left.
Dee escapes all liability once she leaves the partnership.
Dee is liable for every partnership debt, whenever incurred, before or after she left.
Dee is liable only if she knew of the debt before she left.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Dissociation does not discharge liability for obligations incurred while she was a partner (RUPA § 703), absent a release by the creditor.
Leaving does not discharge existing obligations.
She is not liable for debts incurred after she left, except under the two-year lingering-liability rule.
Knowledge does not matter.
A is correct.

q: In MJ & Partners Restaurant LP v. Zadikoff, the court allowed the breach-of-fiduciary-duty claim to proceed even though Zadikoff's contracts called him an "outside consultant," because:
o: Agency turns on actual practices like control and power to bind, not labels.
Consultants always owe fiduciary duties to the clients they advise.
Zadikoff was in substance a partner in the restaurant business.
Zadikoff had signed a separate non-compete agreement with the restaurant's owners.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Agency turns on the parties' actual practices, such as the right to control and the power to bind, not on contract labels. Zadikoff ran the restaurant day to day, so he could be an agent who owed loyalty.
No such categorical rule exists.
The issue was agency, not partnership.
The claim rested on fiduciary duty, not a non-compete.
A is correct.

q: Which of the following best distinguishes Giles v. Giles Land Co. from Owen v. Cohen?
o: Giles was decided under the UPA, while Owen was decided under the RUPA.
Owen held that a partner's misconduct is never a ground for court-ordered dissolution.
Giles expelled the disruptive partner and kept the business going; Owen dissolved.
Giles required a unanimous vote of the other partners to expel him.
None of the above.
oe: Reversed: Owen is a 1941 UPA-era case; Giles applied RUPA.
Owen affirmed a court-ordered dissolution for persistent misconduct.

Correct. In Giles the court expelled the disruptive partner and the business continued; in Owen the court dissolved the partnership. RUPA lets a court remove one partner, with a buyout, instead of dissolving the whole business.
Giles was a judicial expulsion.
C is correct.

q: Under Restatement (Third) of Agency § 8.06, a principal's consent to conduct by an agent that would otherwise breach the duty of loyalty is effective if the agent:
o: Acts in good faith.
Discloses all material facts that the agent knows, has reason to know, or should know would reasonably affect the principal's judgment.
Deals fairly with the principal, and the consent concerns a specific act or type of act.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Required.
Required.
Required.
Incomplete.
Correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Effective consent (§ 8.06)

q: In Sonet v. Plum Creek Timber Co., L.P., the Delaware Court of Chancery dismissed the unitholder's claim because:
o: General partners never owe fiduciary duties under Delaware law.
A clear agreement displaced default duties and left the matter to a unitholder vote.
The conversion was entirely fair to the limited partners.
The court followed Jerman v. O'Leary and read the clause narrowly against the unitholder.
None of the above.
oe: Delaware imposes default fiduciary duties, but a clear agreement can displace them.

Correct. A clear partnership agreement displaces default fiduciary duties, and this agreement let the general partner propose the conversion subject to a two-thirds unitholder vote: "the ballot box, not the courthouse." This is Delaware's contract-first approach to LPs.
The court did not reach entire fairness.
Jerman (Arizona) read duties into a permissive clause, the contrasting approach.
B is correct.

q: Under Sandvick v. LaCrosse, which of the following are elements of a joint venture?
o: Contributions of money, property, time, or skill, which need not be equal.
A proprietary interest in, and mutual control over, the subject of the venture.
A continuing business with no defined end.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: An element.
An element.
Not an element. A joint venture is a limited undertaking; Sandvick was a single deal, not an ongoing business.
Correct. The other elements are an agreement to share profits (usually losses) and an express or implied contract.
C is not an element.

q: In Kleeman v. Rheingold, the lawyer could be held liable for the process server's botched service because:
o: The process server was the lawyer's employee, not a contractor.
A lawyer's duty to serve process properly is nondelegable.
The lawyer negligently selected an unreliable process server.
Serving process is an inherently dangerous activity.
None of the above.
oe: The process server was an independent contractor.
Correct. Some duties are too important to delegate (R3d § 7.06), so hiring an independent server did not shift the responsibility.
The holding rests on nondelegability, not negligent selection.
Not an inherently dangerous activity.
B is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lakeview Hospital operates an emergency department. Its emergency physicians, including Dr. Mora, practice through their own medical corporations under contracts calling them "independent contractors." Lakeview's signs and advertisements say "Lakeview Emergency Care — Our Doctors Are Here 24/7." Patients are not told that the physicians are independent, except for a disclaimer in small print on page 6 of an admission packet. Paramedics bring Ellis, unconscious after a car crash, to Lakeview, where Dr. Mora treats him negligently.

Ellis sues Lakeview. Under Williams v. Dimensions Health Corp., which of the following statements is true?
o: Lakeview cannot be liable, because Dr. Mora's contract calls her an independent contractor.
Lakeview cannot be liable, because Ellis was unconscious and chose nothing.
Lakeview may be vicariously liable for Dr. Mora as its apparent agent.
Lakeview is liable only if it negligently selected or retained Dr. Mora.
None of the above.
oe: The label does not defeat apparent agency.
The majority held that patients look to the facility. The dissent would have required the patient's own belief.

Correct. Under R2d § 267, a hospital may be vicariously liable for its apparent agent based on its holding out of emergency physicians, the patient's reliance on the facility, and the reasonableness of that reliance.
Apparent agency is an independent route to liability.
C is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lakeview Hospital operates an emergency department. Its emergency physicians, including Dr. Mora, practice through their own medical corporations under contracts calling them "independent contractors." Lakeview's signs and advertisements say "Lakeview Emergency Care — Our Doctors Are Here 24/7." Patients are not told that the physicians are independent, except for a disclaimer in small print on page 6 of an admission packet. Paramedics bring Ellis, unconscious after a car crash, to Lakeview, where Dr. Mora treats him negligently.

Lakeview argues that the disclaimer in the admission packet defeats any apparent agency. What is the best response?
o: A disclaimer is never relevant to apparent agency in a hospital case.
A disclaimer must be meaningful, and one Ellis never saw or signed is not.
Any written disclaimer defeats apparent agency as a matter of law.
The disclaimer turns Ellis's claim into one for estoppel rather than agency.
None of the above.
oe: Overstated. A meaningful, timely disclaimer can matter.

Correct. A disclaimer buried in a packet that an unconscious patient never saw or signed does not defeat apparent agency. Williams: the disclaimer in the unsigned consent form did not help the hospital.
Williams rejected that.
The claim remains apparent agency in tort.
B is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lakeview Hospital operates an emergency department. Its emergency physicians, including Dr. Mora, practice through their own medical corporations under contracts calling them "independent contractors." Lakeview's signs and advertisements say "Lakeview Emergency Care — Our Doctors Are Here 24/7." Patients are not told that the physicians are independent, except for a disclaimer in small print on page 6 of an admission packet. Paramedics bring Ellis, unconscious after a car crash, to Lakeview, where Dr. Mora treats him negligently.

Which of the following statements about Dr. Mora's own liability is true?
o: Dr. Mora is personally liable for her own negligence.
Following Lakeview's protocols would not by itself be a defense.
Dr. Mora is liable only if Lakeview is insolvent.
None of the above.
A and B.
oe: True. An agent is always liable for its own torts (R3d § 7.01).
True. Following orders is no defense to the agent's own tort.
False. Her liability is independent and joint with Lakeview's.
A and B are true.
Correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lakeview Hospital operates an emergency department. Its emergency physicians, including Dr. Mora, practice through their own medical corporations under contracts calling them "independent contractors." Lakeview's signs and advertisements say "Lakeview Emergency Care — Our Doctors Are Here 24/7." Patients are not told that the physicians are independent, except for a disclaimer in small print on page 6 of an admission packet. Paramedics bring Ellis, unconscious after a car crash, to Lakeview, where Dr. Mora treats him negligently.

Suppose Lakeview knew that Dr. Mora had lost her privileges at two other hospitals for repeated negligence, but contracted with her anyway. What additional theory does Ellis have against Lakeview?
o: Direct liability for negligently selecting or retaining her.
Ratification of her treatment.
Inherent agency power.
Estoppel based on Ellis's reliance on the hospital.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. R3d § 7.05; it is also an exception to the independent-contractor rule.
Nothing suggests Lakeview affirmed the negligent treatment.
That doctrine concerns contracts with third parties.
Estoppel requires the plaintiff's detrimental reliance, which is not the theory here.
A is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Lakeview Hospital operates an emergency department. Its emergency physicians, including Dr. Mora, practice through their own medical corporations under contracts calling them "independent contractors." Lakeview's signs and advertisements say "Lakeview Emergency Care — Our Doctors Are Here 24/7." Patients are not told that the physicians are independent, except for a disclaimer in small print on page 6 of an admission packet. Which of the following is a rationale for imposing vicarious liability on Lakeview?
o: Risk spreading: Lakeview can insure against the loss and spread its cost.
Safety incentives: Lakeview can reduce harm through how it selects and monitors physicians.
Fault: vicarious liability requires proof that Lakeview itself was negligent.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A recognized rationale.
A recognized rationale.
False. Respondeat superior is strict liability without fault (Kerl).
Correct. Other rationales include control, enterprise liability (Bushey), and the principal's vouching for its agents (Kidd).
C is wrong.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Faye, Gil, and Hal are partners in FGH Bistro, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their agreement includes a buyout clause: when a partner dies, the surviving partners "shall purchase the deceased partner's interest for the balance of his capital account." Hal's estate argues that the buyout price should reflect the market value of the building. Under G & S Investments v. Belman, which of the following statements is true?
o: The estate receives market value, because "capital account" means fair value.
The clause is void, because it is unfair to Hal's estate.
The clause is enforced as written, using the capital account at cost.
The estate may force a liquidation of the partnership instead.
None of the above.
oe: G & S rejected that reading.
Courts enforce buyout clauses as written.
Correct. "Capital account" means the figure on the partnership's books, kept at cost. This is the danger of book-value formulas.
The agreement provides for a buyout and continuation.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Book-value buyout

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Faye, Gil, and Hal are partners in FGH Bistro, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their agreement includes a buyout clause: when a partner dies, the surviving partners "shall purchase the deceased partner's interest for the balance of his capital account." The bistro's building has greatly appreciated, but the partnership keeps its capital accounts at cost. Hal dies.

Hal contributed $40,000 when the partnership was formed. Over the years, his share of partnership profits totaled $160,000, and he took draws totaling $150,000. What is the balance of Hal's capital account?
oe: That ignores profits and draws.
That ignores draws.
Draws reduce the capital account; they are not added to it.
Correct. Contributions plus profits minus losses minus draws: $40,000 + $160,000 − $150,000 = $50,000.
That leaves out the contribution.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Capital account math

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Faye, Gil, and Hal are partners in FGH Bistro, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their agreement includes a buyout clause: when a partner dies, the surviving partners "shall purchase the deceased partner's interest for the balance of his capital account." The bistro's building has greatly appreciated, but the partnership keeps its capital accounts at cost. Hal dies.

Suppose instead that FGH Bistro had no buyout clause and no fixed term. Under the RUPA, what is the effect of Hal's death?
o: Hal is dissociated, and the partnership continues and buys out his interest.
The partnership automatically dissolves on Hal's death and must be wound up.
Hal's estate becomes a partner in Hal's place.
The partnership must hold a liquidation sale of its assets.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under RUPA, death is a dissociation that does not dissolve an at-will firm; § 801(1) covers only a partner's express will to withdraw.
That is the UPA rule.
An estate does not become a partner.
No sale is required.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Death in an at-will firm

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Faye, Gil, and Hal are partners in FGH Bistro, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their agreement includes a buyout clause: when a partner dies, the surviving partners "shall purchase the deceased partner's interest for the balance of his capital account." The bistro's building has greatly appreciated, but the partnership keeps its capital accounts at cost. Hal dies.

Suppose Hal's widow demands that the bistro's assets be sold at a liquidation sale so the estate can be paid. Under Creel v. Lilly, which of the following statements is true?
o: Winding up always requires a forced sale of all the bistro's assets.
A forced sale isn't required; a good-faith valuation and payment is enough.
The widow becomes a partner and may vote on whether to sell.
The survivors must pay the estate the building's full market value plus goodwill.
None of the above.
oe: Creel rejected that.

Correct. Winding up is not the same as a fire sale: a good-faith inventory, valuation, and payment of the estate's share is enough. Creel marks the shift from aggregate-theory dissolution to entity continuity.
An estate does not become a partner.
Creel required a fair, good-faith accounting, not a premium.
B is correct.

q: In Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, Inc., Judge Learned Hand held Edison bound to its contract with the singer because:
o: Fuller had express actual authority to hire the singer for a fully unconditional concert tour.
Hiring singers was within the customary scope of Fuller's job, and the limit was secret.
Edison later ratified the contract by accepting the singer's services.
The singer was Edison's employee rather than Fuller's.
None of the above.
oe: Fuller's secret instructions limited him to recitals dealers later booked.

Correct. Hiring singers without such an unusual condition was within the customary scope of Fuller's job, the limit was never communicated, and a principal who chooses an agent "vouches" for him. Third parties may rely on the customary scope of an agent's role.
Edison refused to pay.
Employment status was not the issue.
B is correct.

q: Which case held that "income partners," who received fixed salaries and bonuses, shared no profits or losses, and could not vote, were not partners and so were not vicariously liable for the firm's malpractice?
o: Zajac v. Harris.
Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long.
Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co.
Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates v. Wells.
Davis v. Loftus.
oe: Zajac found a partnership based on a capital contribution and an equal share of all profits.
Kaufman-Brown found that distributors who shared profits and losses were partners.
Frank enforced a book-value buyout understanding.
Clackamas addressed whether owner-physicians were employees under the ADA.
Correct. Profit sharing and control define real partners; titles do not.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — "Income partners"

q: Under the RUPA, which of the following may a partnership agreement NOT vary?
o: A partner's power to dissociate by express will.
The default rule that partners share profits equally.
A court's power to order dissolution on a partner's application, on the statutory grounds.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: Not variable. The agreement may require written notice but cannot eliminate the power.
Freely variable.
Not variable (§ 105(c)).
Correct. The agreement may modify the other dissolution events but not the court-ordered grounds.
B is variable.

q: In Day v. Sidley & Austin, the court rejected the senior partner's claims because:
o: The agreement let the executive committee and a majority control the merger.
Partnership law requires unanimous consent for a merger, and Day had voted for it.
Day had no standing to sue because he had already resigned.
Partners owe one another no duty of disclosure about firm management.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The partnership agreement gave the executive committee control of firm policy and let a majority approve the merger, and fiduciary duty does not require disclosing internal changes that bring no profit to the other partners and no loss to the firm. Partners can contract around the defaults of unanimity and equal management; a "bruised ego" is not a claim.
Day's vote was not the basis of the decision; the agreement controlled.
The court reached the merits.
Partners do owe disclosure duties; this nondisclosure did not breach them.
A is correct.

q: In Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians & Employers' Pension Fund v. Steven Scott Enterprises, Inc., the fund was bound to all 15 settlement agreements its trustee signed. On what grounds?
o: Apparent authority, until the employer learned that only the board could settle.
Estoppel, because the employer relied on the trustee's signature.
Ratification, because the fund knowingly cashed the checks and never objected.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: A ground.
A ground.
A ground.
Incomplete.
Correct. One fact pattern shows all three theories, and notice of the real limits ends reasonable reliance.

q: Which of the following is a ground for judicial dissolution of an LLC on a member's application under the ULLCA, but has no counterpart in the RUPA's grounds for dissolving a partnership?
o: The company's activities have become unlawful under state law.
It is not reasonably practicable to carry on the company's activities.
Those in control have acted oppressively and directly harmed the applicant.
A member has expressed the will to withdraw from the company.
None of the above.
oe: Both statutes address unlawful activity.
Both statutes have a "not reasonably practicable" ground.
Correct. Oppression by the managers or members in control is an LLC ground (§ 701) with no RUPA counterpart, and the court may order a lesser remedy.
In an LLC, withdrawal does not dissolve the company.
C is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ike, Joy, and Ken are partners in IJK Hardware, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Ike and Joy each contributed $20,000; Ken contributed only services. They share profits equally. Joy also lent the partnership $10,000. On June 1, Ike gives the others written notice of his express will to withdraw. The partners do not agree to continue the business. On June 5, Joy files a statement of dissolution with the secretary of state.

What is the effect of Ike's notice?
o: The partnership is dissolved and must be wound up.
Ike is bought out under Article 7, and the business continues.
Ike's withdrawal is wrongful and makes him liable for damages.
Ike's withdrawal is ineffective without the other partners' consent.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In an at-will partnership, a partner's express will to withdraw is a dissolution event (§ 801(1)).
Dissolution, not a buyout, follows an express-will withdrawal from an at-will firm.
Nothing makes it wrongful: there is no term and no breach of an express provision.
A partner always has the power to dissociate.
A is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ike, Joy, and Ken are partners in IJK Hardware, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Ike and Joy each contributed $20,000; Ken contributed only services. They share profits equally. Joy also lent the partnership $10,000. On June 1, Ike gives the others written notice of his express will to withdraw. The partners do not agree to continue the business. On June 5, Joy files a statement of dissolution with the secretary of state.

During winding up, which of the following acts is appropriate for winding up the partnership's business?

Hiring new staff to expand the business during winding up.
Collecting receivables and completing orders pending at dissolution.
Launching a new line of power tools to attract buyers.
None of the above.
oe: That is new business, not winding up.
That is new business.
Correct. Winding up means concluding unfinished business, paying debts, and distributing what remains.
That is new business.
C is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ike, Joy, and Ken are partners in IJK Hardware, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Ike and Joy each contributed $20,000; Ken contributed only services. They share profits equally. Joy also lent the partnership $10,000. On June 1, Ike gives the others written notice of his express will to withdraw. The partners do not agree to continue the business. On June 5, Joy files a statement of dissolution with the secretary of state.

On July 1, Ken orders $20,000 of the store's usual inventory on credit from a supplier that knows nothing about the dissolution. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The partnership may be bound, because the supplier lacked notice of the dissolution, and the filed statement does not give constructive notice until 90 days after June 5.
Ken is liable to the other partners for any loss caused by knowingly binding the partnership to new business.
The statement of dissolution gave the supplier notice as soon as it was filed.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. Constructive notice arises 90 days after filing.
Correct.
C is wrong.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ike, Joy, and Ken are partners in IJK Hardware, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Ike and Joy each contributed $20,000; Ken contributed only services. They share profits equally. Joy also lent the partnership $10,000. On June 1, Ike gives the others written notice of his express will to withdraw. The partners do not agree to continue the business. On June 5, Joy files a statement of dissolution with the secretary of state.

IJK's assets sell for $100,000. It owes outside creditors $40,000 and owes Joy the $10,000 loan. Under the RUPA's distribution rules, how much does each partner receive in total?
o: Each partner receives $16,667.
None of the above.
oe: Ken has no capital to return, and the $10,000 surplus is split three ways.

Correct. Pay all creditors, including Joy's $10,000 loan ($50,000 in all). Return contributions ($20,000 each to Ike and Joy). Split the $10,000 surplus equally ($3,333 each). Joy's total includes her loan repayment.
Creditors and contributions are paid before any equal split.
Ken shares equally in profits even though he contributed no capital.
B is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Ike, Joy, and Ken are partners in IJK Hardware, a general partnership governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997), with no fixed term. Ike and Joy each contributed $20,000; Ken contributed only services. They share profits equally. Joy also lent the partnership $10,000. On June 1, Ike gives the others written notice of his express will to withdraw. The partners do not agree to continue the business. On June 5, Joy files a statement of dissolution with the secretary of state.

During winding up, the partners agree to auction IJK's most valuable asset, an exclusive distribution contract, to Joy. Ken then secretly competes for the contract himself and wins it. Under Monin v. Monin, which of the following statements is true?
o: Ken breached his fiduciary duty, which continues through winding up.
Ken committed no breach, because partners owe no duties after dissolution.
Ken may compete for it, because the partnership has dissolved.
Ken is liable only for breach of the auction agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Dissolution does not free a partner to take the firm's key asset.
Duties continue through winding up.
Not for the partnership's own asset during winding up.
Monin found a breach of fiduciary duty and awarded damages.
A is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Fund, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership. Its only general partner is Summit GP, Inc., a corporation owned by Tia and Ugo, who are also limited partners. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may buy partnership assets "in its sole discretion," and that conflicted transactions approved in good faith by a conflicts committee of independent directors "shall not be a breach of any duty."

Summit Fund breaches a supply contract with Vend Co., which knew it was dealing with an LP whose general partner was a corporation. Vend sues Tia and Ugo personally. Under Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, Inc., which of the following statements is true?
o: They are personally liable, because they own and control the corporate general partner.
They are not personally liable, because they acted only for the corporate general partner.
They are liable as general partners, because they run Summit GP.
They are liable only up to their capital contributions as limited partners.
None of the above.
oe: Frigidaire rejected that theory.

Correct. They acted only as officers of the corporate general partner, and Vend knew it was dealing with the corporation; the remedy for undercapitalization is veil piercing. A corporate general partner gives everyone in an LP limited liability.
Summit GP, Inc. is the general partner, not Tia and Ugo.
Their contributions are at risk as limited partners, but they are not personally liable.
B is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Fund, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership. Its only general partner is Summit GP, Inc., a corporation owned by Tia and Ugo, who are also limited partners. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may buy partnership assets "in its sole discretion," and that conflicted transactions approved in good faith by a conflicts committee of independent directors "shall not be a breach of any duty."

Summit GP buys a parcel from Summit Fund, relying on an appraisal that ignored a favorable rezoning of the land. Under Jerman v. O'Leary, which of the following statements is true?
o: The "sole discretion" clause eliminates all fiduciary duties, so there is no claim.
A general partner can never buy partnership property from the fund.
The clause allows the purchase, but Summit GP still owes fair value and disclosure.
The purchase requires a vote of the limited partners to be valid.
None of the above.
oe: Jerman did not read the clause that way.
The clause allowed the purchase.
Correct. The general partner still must pay fair value and disclose the facts bearing on value. Courts may read fiduciary duties into permissive agreements (contrast Sonet).
Nothing required a vote.
C is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Fund, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership. Its only general partner is Summit GP, Inc., a corporation owned by Tia and Ugo, who are also limited partners. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may buy partnership assets "in its sole discretion," and that conflicted transactions approved in good faith by a conflicts committee of independent directors "shall not be a breach of any duty."

The conflicts committee, acting in subjective good faith, approves Summit GP's sale of one of its own assets to Summit Fund. A unitholder sues for breach of fiduciary duty. Under In re El Paso Pipeline Partners, L.P. Derivative Litigation, which of the following statements is true?
o: Entire-fairness review always applies to a controller's deal with a Delaware LP, whatever the agreement says.
Delaware forbids partnership agreements from replacing default fiduciary duties.
The transaction requires unanimous approval of the unitholders to stand.
The contractual standard governs, because Delaware lets the agreement replace fiduciary duties.
None of the above.
oe: The agreement replaced default duties.
Delaware allows it.
The agreement sets the approval process.

Correct. Delaware lets an alternative-entity agreement replace default fiduciary duties, and investors may get only the contract's protections. The committee was not liable for information it never had.
D is correct.

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Summit Fund, L.P. is a Delaware limited partnership. Its only general partner is Summit GP, Inc., a corporation owned by Tia and Ugo, who are also limited partners. The partnership agreement provides that the general partner may buy partnership assets "in its sole discretion," and that conflicted transactions approved in good faith by a conflicts committee of independent directors "shall not be a breach of any duty."

The agreement also bars partners from operating any fund that invests in "Delaware timberland," a narrowly defined term. Tia starts a fund that invests in Maryland timberland. Under Cincinnati SMSA L.P. v. Cincinnati Bell Cellular Systems Co., which of the following statements is true?
o: No breach; the implied covenant won't expand a precise, unambiguous non-compete.
The implied covenant expands the non-compete to cover substantially similar businesses.
Tia breached her duty of loyalty to the fund as a limited partner.
Tia breached the agreement because Maryland timberland is similar.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The implied covenant is a narrow gap-filler (compare Nemec).
Cincinnati SMSA rejected that.
Limited partners generally owe no fiduciary duties solely by reason of that status.
The clause is limited to its terms.
A is correct.

q: Under the "equal dignities" rule:
o: Authority to sign a contract within the Statute of Frauds must be in writing.
Every agency relationship, however informal, must be created in a signed writing.
The principal and the agent must have equal contractual capacity.
An agent must be paid the same as the principal's other agents.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. If the agent will sign a contract that the Statute of Frauds requires to be in writing, such as a contract for the sale of land, the agent's authority generally must also be in writing. A writing is otherwise generally not required, and a principal may be estopped to deny the missing writing (R3d § 3.02).
Agency generally requires no writing.
The agent needs only minimal capacity.
No such rule exists.
A is correct.

q: Which of the following terminates an agent's actual authority?
o: The principal's death.
Notice by either party that it is ending the relationship.
The agent's breach of fiduciary duty.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Terminates by operation of law.
Terminates it. Either party has the power to end the relationship, even if not the right.
Terminates it.
Incomplete.

Correct. Other terminating events include agreement, the purpose being fulfilled, lapse of a reasonable time, and changed circumstances. Ending actual authority does not automatically end apparent authority.

q: In Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long, the potato distributors were held to be partners rather than creditors of the growers primarily because:
o: They lent money to the growers to finance the crop.
They shared both profits and losses and acted like co-owners.
They signed written loan documents with the growers.
They had a veto over the growers' speculative transactions.
None of the above.
oe: Lending alone points toward creditor status.
Correct. Compare Martin v. Peyton: sharing losses and co-owner conduct tip the balance toward partnership.
Documents labeled as loans did not save them.
That kind of protective term was what kept the Martin v. Peyton lenders from being partners.
B is correct.

q: In Young v. Jones, the court rejected the investors' claim that the U.S. Price Waterhouse firm was liable as a partner by estoppel of the Bahamas firm because:
o: Partnership by estoppel no longer exists under modern partnership statutes.
The firms' worldwide advertising was itself a representation of partnership.
The plaintiffs never relied on any representation that the firms were partners.
The Bahamas firm's audit letter turned out to be accurate.
None of the above.
oe: It exists under both UPA § 16 and RUPA § 308.
The court did not find reliance on any such representation.
Correct. Partnership by estoppel requires a representation and reliance.
The letter was fraudulent.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Young v. Jones

q: Which of the following statements is consistent with Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray and Bohatch v. Butler & Binion?
o: Partners may expel a partner under a negotiated no-cause expulsion clause, in good faith, as long as nothing owed to the expelled partner is wrongfully withheld.
Partners owe no fiduciary duty not to expel a partner for reporting suspected overbilling by another partner.
Expelling a partner always breaches the duty of loyalty.
None of the above.
A and B.
oe: Consistent with Lawlis.
Consistent with Bohatch.
Inconsistent with both cases.
A and B are consistent.
Correct. Courts enforce "guillotine" expulsion clauses as written, and partners may part ways when trust breaks down.

q: In Meehan v. Shaughnessy, the departing partners breached their duty of loyalty by:
o: Unfairly acquiring client consents, including denying their plans when asked.
Secretly planning to start a new firm while they were still partners there.
Leaving the firm before their partnership agreement's term had expired.
Renting office space for the new firm before giving notice.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. They denied their plans when asked, prepared client letters on the old firm's letterhead, and rushed to sign up clients the moment they gave notice. They had to prove clients would have come anyway or hold the profits from those cases in trust for the old firm.
Preparing to leave was permitted.
Leaving was not the breach.
Permitted preparation.
A is correct.

At a Petro-operated station, a Petro clerk shouts racial slurs at a customer while ringing up the customer's purchase. Under Arguello v. Conoco, Inc., which of the following statements is true?
o: The clerk's conduct is outside the scope of employment as a matter of law, because racist abuse never serves the employer.
Whether the clerk's abuse during the sale was within the scope of employment is a question for the jury.
Petro ratified the abuse by counseling the clerk afterward.
Agency and scope rules do not apply to statutory civil-rights claims.
None of the above.
oe: Arguello held this was a jury question.
Correct. The clerk was doing her job (the sale) when the abuse occurred.
Arguello held that counseling was not ratification.
Arguello applied them to statutory claims.
B is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Petro Corp. sells gasoline under the "Petro Express" brand. It owns and operates some stations itself, staffed by Petro employees. Other Petro Express stations are owned by independent dealers who license the brand and buy Petro fuel, but who set their own hours, hire and pay their own staff, and keep their own profits.

The same abuse occurs at an independently owned Petro Express station, by the dealer's own employee. Under Arguello, which of the following statements is true?
o: Petro is liable, because the station displays the Petro Express brand.
Petro is liable, because it supplies the station's fuel under contract.
Petro is not liable, because it did not control the dealer's daily operations.
Petro is liable under the inherently dangerous activity exception.
None of the above.

Being a supplier is not control.
Correct. The branded dealers were not Petro's agents: Petro did not control their daily operations or their staff. Owned and branded outlets differ.
That exception concerns physical risks of the work.
C is correct.

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Petro Corp. sells gasoline under the "Petro Express" brand. It owns and operates some stations itself, staffed by Petro employees. Other Petro Express stations are owned by independent dealers who license the brand and buy Petro fuel, but who set their own hours, hire and pay their own staff, and keep their own profits.

Comparing Humble Oil & Refining Co. v. Martin with Hoover v. Sun Oil Co., which set of facts would most likely make a station operator Petro's servant?
o: Petro owns the station, sets the hours, and can end the deal and reassign the operator at will.
The dealer sets his own hours, hires and pays his own staff, and bears the profits and losses.
Petro's representative visits weekly with suggestions that the dealer is free to ignore.
B and C.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. These are the Humble facts (Petro owns the station and its products, sets the hours, pays most utilities, can end the arrangement at will, and can assign other duties), where the operator was a servant despite a contract calling him independent.
Those are the Hoover facts, where the dealer was an independent contractor.
Advice the dealer may ignore is not control (Hoover).
Both describe independence.
A is correct.
