q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Petro Corp. sells gasoline under the "Petro Express" brand. It owns and operates some stations itself, staffed by Petro employees. Other Petro Express stations are owned by independent dealers who license the brand and buy Petro fuel, but who set their own hours, hire and pay their own staff, and keep their own profits.

At a Petro-operated station, a drunk customer argues with Lou, a Petro attendant, about paying for gas, then punches Lou. Lou hits back and injures the customer. Under the reasoning of Lamkin v. Brooks, which of the following statements is true?
o: The fight was purely personal, so it is outside the scope of employment.
Intentional torts like battery are never within the scope of employment.
Petro is liable only if it later ratified Lou's conduct.
Violence closely tied to the employee's duties can be within scope.
None of the above.

They can be.
Scope of employment is enough.

Correct. Violence closely connected in time, place, and causation to the employee's duties can be within the scope of employment. In Lamkin, a police officer's fight arising from his response to a complaint was employment-rooted.

Q7–11 HYPO: Petro Corp. sells gasoline under the "Petro Express" brand. It owns and operates some stations itself, staffed by Petro employees. Under the "better standard" policy approach to vicarious liability discussed in class, which questions help decide whether Petro should bear a loss caused by its employee?
o: Should either party have anticipated precautions against the loss?
Could either party have taken cost-effective precautions?
If both could have, which party could have done so at the lowest cost?
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Part of the analysis.
Part of the analysis.
Part of the analysis.
Incomplete.
Correct. The goal is to minimize the sum of accident losses and precaution costs by placing liability on the party who could prevent the loss most cheaply.

Lena claims a share of the $60,000 recovery. Under Putnam v. Shoaf, which of the following statements is true?
o: Lena receives one-third of the recovery, because the embezzlement occurred while she was a partner.
Lena receives the part of the recovery traceable to her own capital.
Lena may rescind the sale of her interest.
Lena receives nothing, because the claims belonged to the partnership and she sold her interest.
None of the above.
oe: Putnam rejected this.
The claims were not divided among the partners.
There was no basis for rescission in Putnam.
Correct. A partner owns an interest in the partnership, not in specific assets. Selling a partnership interest sells everything, including unknown claims.
D is correct.

o: Without demand, any information concerning the partnership's business and affairs reasonably required for the proper exercise of the partner's rights and duties.
On demand, any other information concerning the partnership's business and affairs, unless the demand or the information demanded is unreasonable or otherwise improper.
Only when the other partner asks in writing.
None of the above.
A and B.
oe: True.
True.
False. Some information must be furnished without any demand.
A and B are true.
Correct. Information that a partner reasonably needs must be furnished without demand; other information must be furnished on demand.

The partners, as tenants in partnership.
The partners individually, by capital.
Whoever was a partner at the time.
None of the above.

Partners have no interest in specific partnership property.
Ownership is the entity's, not that of the partners at a given time.

Absent agreement, a new partner needs the consent of all the partners.
Nia can transfer her interest to her son, which makes him a partner.
Max's objection doesn't matter, because admitting a partner is an ordinary business matter.
None of the above.

Correct. RUPA § 402; UPA § 18(g).
A transferee is not a partner.
Admission is not ordinary business.

q: In Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership, LLP, the settlement was enforceable against the plaintiffs through their lawyer's apparent authority because:
o: Hiring a lawyer, by itself, gives the lawyer apparent authority to settle.
The clients' own conduct at the mediation held the lawyer out as authorized.
The lawyer repeatedly assured opposing counsel that he had authority.
The clients ratified the settlement in writing after the mediation.
None of the above.
oe: The court said hiring a lawyer alone is not enough.

Correct. The clients' conduct (attending the mediation, conferring with the lawyer during the final talks, and never limiting his authority) held him out as authorized, and opposing counsel reasonably believed him. Apparent authority can come from the principal's conduct and silence.
An agent's own statements can bolster reasonableness but cannot alone create apparent authority.
They repudiated it.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ackerman v. Sobol

q: In Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh, Thornburgh was held personally liable for his campaign committee's unpaid bill because:
o: Candidates are always personally liable for their campaigns' debts.
The committee was his alter ego, so the court pierced its veil.
His aide, an agent he controlled, approved the contract on his behalf.
He personally signed the fundraising contract with the firm.
None of the above.
oe: There is no such categorical rule.
The court relied on agency, not veil piercing.

Correct. A member of an unincorporated association is bound by contracts he authorized, assented to, or ratified, personally or through an agent, and his aide Dickman, his controlled agent, approved the contract. Control is the key to finding agency despite denials.
He did not sign it; his agent approved it.
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Karl Rove v. Thornburgh

q: Nogales Service Center v. Atlantic Richfield Co. explained that inherent authority differs from apparent authority because inherent authority:
o: Arises from the agency relationship itself, with no manifestation to the third party.
Requires a manifestation by the principal to the third party about the agent's authority.
Requires the principal's later ratification of the agent's act.
Applies only to undisclosed principals, never to disclosed ones.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under R2d § 161, a general agent can bind the principal to acts usual in his authorized dealings, even if forbidden.
That describes apparent authority.
Inherent authority does not depend on ratification.
Section 161 covers general agents of disclosed principals; §§ 194–195 cover undisclosed principals.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Nogales (inherent authority)

q: The Restatement (Third) of Agency abandons inherent agency power. Under § 2.06, which of the following statements is true of an undisclosed principal?
o: It is liable to a third party who justifiably relies to its detriment on an unauthorized agent's conduct if the principal, on notice of that conduct, failed to take reasonable steps to notify the third party of the facts.
It may not rely on instructions that reduce the agent's authority below what the third party would assume if the principal were disclosed.
It is liable only if the third party knew the principal's identity.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. By definition, the third party does not know the undisclosed principal's identity.
Correct. These are the narrower, estoppel-like replacements for Watteau's rule.
C is wrong.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — R3d § 2.06

q: Which of the following is NOT a factor under Restatement (Second) of Agency § 220(2) in deciding whether a worker is a servant?
o: The extent of control the employer may exercise over the details of the work.
Whether the employer or the worker supplies the tools and the place of work.
Whether the worker is paid by the hour or by the job.
Whether the work is part of the employer's regular business.
Whether the worker has ever been sued for negligence.
oe: A § 220 factor.
A § 220 factor.
A § 220 factor.
A § 220 factor.
Correct: NOT a factor. The others also include skill, a distinct occupation, length of employment, the parties' belief, and whether the principal is in business.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — R2d § 220 factors

q: Under the Restatement (Second) of Agency, which of the following statements about forbidden and criminal acts is true?
o: An act may be within the scope of employment even though it is forbidden or done in a forbidden manner.
A consciously tortious or criminal act may be within the scope of employment, though serious crimes usually are not.
Any act that violates an express employer rule is outside the scope of employment.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. Forbidden acts can be within scope.
Correct.
C is wrong.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Forbidden and criminal acts

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Owen and his wife Penny co-own a 100-acre farm. Without consulting Penny, Owen signs a five-year lease of the entire farm to Quill, including an option to buy, signing only his own name. Penny sees Quill farming the land, and Owen deposits the rent into the couple's joint account. Quill later learns that Penny is a co-owner and tries to exercise the option against both of them.

Quill argues that Owen acted as Penny's agent in signing the lease. Under Botticello v. Stefanovicz, which of the following statements is true?
o: Penny is bound, because spouses are each other's agents.
Penny is bound, because co-owners of land are each other's agents.
Penny is not bound on an agency theory, because Quill can't prove Owen was her agent.
Penny is bound, because she benefited from the rent Quill paid.
None of the above.
oe: Marriage does not make one spouse the other's agent.
Co-ownership does not create agency.
Correct. Marriage and co-ownership alone do not make one spouse the other's agent, and the party asserting agency must prove it.
Benefit may matter to ratification, not to whether an agency existed.
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Botticello: no agency

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Owen and his wife Penny co-own a 100-acre farm. Without consulting Penny, Owen signs a five-year lease of the entire farm to Quill, including an option to buy, signing only his own name. Penny sees Quill farming the land, and Owen deposits the rent into the couple's joint account. Quill later learns that Penny is a co-owner and tries to exercise the option against both of them.

Quill argues that Penny ratified the lease and option. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Penny ratified by receiving rent in the couple's joint account.
Penny did not ratify, because Owen never claimed to act for her.
Penny ratified by her silence after seeing Quill farm the land.
Penny ratified the lease but not the option to buy.
None of the above.
oe: Receiving some rent was not enough in Botticello.

Correct. Ratification requires full knowledge of the material facts and an act done, or purported to be done, on the principal's behalf. Botticello: she lacked full knowledge and intent, and Owen never claimed to act for her.
Silence ratifies only with knowledge and a duty to speak.
There is no partial ratification, and here there was no ratification at all.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Botticello: no ratification

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Owen and his wife Penny co-own a 100-acre farm. Without consulting Penny, Owen signs a five-year lease of the entire farm to Quill, including an option to buy, signing only his own name. Penny sees Quill farming the land, and Owen deposits the rent into the couple's joint account. Quill later learns that Penny is a co-owner and tries to exercise the option against both of them.

Which principle from Ercanbrack v. Crandall-Walker Motor Co. would defeat an argument that a principal ratified a transaction by remaining silent?
o: Silence can ratify only if the principal knows of the transaction.
Silence always ratifies once a reasonable time has passed.
Silence ratifies only if the transaction was in writing.
Silence never ratifies a transaction, whatever the circumstances.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. "Ratification of an act about which the principal knows nothing is inherently impossible." In Ercanbrack, no officer knew of the order, so there was no contract.
Silence without knowledge cannot ratify.
A writing is not the test.
Overstated. Silence can ratify where the principal knows and has a duty to speak.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ercanbrack

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Owen and his wife Penny co-own a 100-acre farm. Without consulting Penny, Owen signs a five-year lease of the entire farm to Quill, including an option to buy, signing only his own name. Penny sees Quill farming the land, and Owen deposits the rent into the couple's joint account. Quill later learns that Penny is a co-owner and tries to exercise the option against both of them.

Suppose Penny had appointed Owen as her agent to manage the farm, and Owen learned that the irrigation well was contaminated. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Owen's knowledge of this material fact is imputed to Penny.
Notice given to an authorized agent is notice to the principal.
Imputation never applies between spouses.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True (R3d § 5.03).
True (R3d § 5.02).
False. There is no spousal exception. Imputation fails mainly when the agent acts adversely to the principal.
Correct.
C is wrong.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Notice and imputed knowledge

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Owen and his wife Penny co-own a 100-acre farm. Without consulting Penny, Owen signs a five-year lease of the entire farm to Quill, including an option to buy, signing only his own name. Penny sees Quill farming the land, and Owen deposits the rent into the couple's joint account. Quill later learns that Penny is a co-owner and tries to exercise the option against both of them.

Assume Penny is not bound by the lease, but half of Quill's rent payments went to her through the joint account. What may Quill do?
o: Enforce the purchase option against Penny for her half.
Hold Penny liable on the implied warranty of authority.
Nothing, because Penny never consented to the lease or anything Owen did.
Hold Penny liable in tort for Owen's misrepresentation.
Seek restitution from Penny to the extent she was unjustly enriched.
oe: She is not bound by the contract.
The warranty runs against the person who purported to act as agent, not the principal.
Unjust enrichment gives a remedy even without consent.
Nothing suggests a tort.
Correct. R3d § 2.07: restitution against a principal unjustly enriched by an agent's act.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Restitution

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rita owns a car-salvage yard. She invites Sam, who cannot read, to join her. Sam borrows $15,000 and uses it to buy wrecked cars for the yard. They split the profits on every car equally, including deals Rita handles alone. Rita's books list Sam as an "employee." They have no written agreement and no agreed term.

Is Sam a partner in the salvage business?
o: Likely not, because Rita's books list him as an employee, not a partner.
Yes, because his capital and equal share of all profits show co-ownership.
No, because he is a lender who is repaid out of the yard's profits on each car.
Yes, but only if he also agreed to share in the yard's losses.
None of the above.
oe: One-sided bookkeeping does not decide the question.
Correct. These are the Zajac v. Harris facts.
Sam bought inventory for the business and shares all profits; he made no loan to Rita.
An agreement to share losses is not required.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Zajac v. Harris

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rita owns a car-salvage yard. She invites Sam, who cannot read, to join her. Sam borrows $15,000 and uses it to buy wrecked cars for the yard. They split the profits on every car equally, including deals Rita handles alone. Rita's books list Sam as an "employee." They have no written agreement and no agreed term.

After years of losses, the yard finally becomes profitable. Rita, who holds a mortgage on the yard, wants to dissolve the partnership so she can take over the business. Under Page v. Page, which of the following statements is true?
o: It is a term partnership lasting until the mortgage is paid off, so dissolving now would be wrongful.
Rita may not dissolve the partnership while it is profitable.
Rita may dissolve the at-will partnership, but only in good faith.
Rita may dissolve and keep the business without accounting to Sam.
None of the above.
oe: A hope of recouping losses or repaying debt does not create an implied term without clear evidence.
Profitability does not bar dissolution of an at-will partnership.
Correct. It is an at-will partnership, so Rita may dissolve it, but she may not use dissolution to freeze Sam out and take the business.
That is the freeze-out Page forbids.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Page v. Page

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rita owns a car-salvage yard. She invites Sam, who cannot read, to join her. Sam borrows $15,000 and uses it to buy wrecked cars for the yard. They split the profits on every car equally, including deals Rita handles alone. Rita's books list Sam as an "employee." They have no written agreement and no agreed term.

Suppose Rita and Sam had agreed that Rita could end Sam's interest at any time by paying him its book value. Rita does so, and Sam sues to force a liquidation sale. Under Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co., which of the following statements is true?
o: Sam can force a liquidation sale, because the UPA gives every partner that right.
The agreement is void, because a partner cannot waive the right to liquidation.
Sam is entitled to the fair market value of his interest.
The agreement controls; Sam receives book value and cannot force a sale.
None of the above.
oe: The UPA's rules are defaults that partners can change.
The agreement was enforced.
The agreement set book value.
Correct.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Frank v. Pickens

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Rita owns a car-salvage yard. She invites Sam, who cannot read, to join her. Sam borrows $15,000 and uses it to buy wrecked cars for the yard. They split the profits on every car equally, including deals Rita handles alone. Rita's books list Sam as an "employee." They have no written agreement and no agreed term.

Suppose the business grows into a 500-partner firm run by a self-perpetuating executive committee, and partners who were demoted claim age discrimination. Under EEOC v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood, which of the following statements is true?
o: State-law partners may still be "employees" under federal law if they lack control.
Partners can never be employees under federal antidiscrimination law.
Anyone who shares profits and has capital at risk is automatically an employer.
The EEOC lacked power to investigate a law firm's internal partnership decisions.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Formal partner status is not the same as actual power (compare Clackamas and Davis).
Sidley rejected that.
The court looked at control, not just profits and capital.
The court allowed the coverage subpoena.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — EEOC v. Sidley

q: Which of the following is NOT an accurate statement of partners' personal liability under the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997)?
o: All partners are jointly and severally liable for all partnership obligations, unless the claimant agrees otherwise or the law provides otherwise.
A partnership creditor generally must exhaust partnership assets before reaching a partner's personal assets.
An incoming partner is not personally liable for partnership obligations incurred before the partner was admitted.
Partners are only jointly, not severally, liable for the partnership's contract obligations.
In an LLP, a partner is not personally liable for partnership obligations incurred while it is an LLP solely by reason of being a partner.
oe: Accurate (§ 306(a)).
Accurate (§ 307).
Accurate (§ 306(b)).
Correct: this is NOT accurate under RUPA. It was the UPA § 15 rule; RUPA makes partners jointly and severally liable for all obligations.
Accurate (§ 306(c)).
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Personal liability under RUPA

q: Under Covalt v. High, when the partners are evenly divided on a matter:
o: The power to act is suspended among the partners, but not as to third parties.
The partner with the larger capital account decides the matter.
A court must step in and dissolve the partnership.
The proposing partner may proceed and bind the others.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. This reconciles National Biscuit (third parties) and Summers (among the partners).
Equal management rights do not depend on capital.
Deadlock alone does not require dissolution.
Internally, the action is blocked.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Covalt v. High

q: In Nemec v. Shrader, the Delaware Supreme Court rejected the retired officers' claim over the book-value redemption of their stock because:
o: The implied covenant of good faith cannot override conduct the contract expressly allows.
The sale of the company was foreseeable, so there was no gap for the implied covenant to fill.
Fiduciary claims are displaced where a contract governs the matter.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A ground of the decision.
A ground of the decision.
A ground of the decision.
Incomplete.
Correct. Insiders are held to their bargains; the implied covenant is a narrow gap-filler. (The dissent would have required the power to serve a legitimate company interest.)
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Nemec v. Shrader

q: In Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan, which conduct by the departing partners was held to be a breach of fiduciary duty?
o: Planning their move to a new firm together while they were still partners.
Giving the new firm confidential salary and billing data before giving notice.
Taking duplicate copies of their desk files when they left.
A and C.
None of the above.
oe: Held not a breach.

Correct. They gave their new firm a confidential memo of their department's staff salaries and billing rates and lined up recruits before giving notice. Confidential information cannot be used for a head start (compare Bancroft-Whitney).
Held not a breach.
Both were held not to be breaches.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott

q: Under the RUPA, absent a contrary agreement, a partner who works full time for the partnership is entitled to:
o: A salary for the time the partner spends working.
Interest on the partner's capital contribution, paid annually.
An equal share of the profits, but no salary for services outside winding up.
A and B.
None of the above.
oe: There is no right to compensation for services by default.
Contributions are returned at their value, without interest, by default.
Correct. RUPA § 401; UPA § 18(f). A partner gets no pay for services except reasonable compensation for winding up the partnership's business.
Neither is a default right.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Compensation and profit shares

q: Under the ULLCA, what may a judgment creditor of an LLC member do?
o: Seize the LLC's property to satisfy the member's personal debt.
Become a member in the debtor's place with full voting rights.
Force the LLC to dissolve and pay the member's share.
Obtain a charging order against the member's transferable interest.
None of the above.
oe: A member's personal creditor cannot reach LLC property.
A creditor does not become a member.
A creditor has no such right.
Correct. ULLCA § 503: a charging order is the creditor's exclusive remedy, except that foreclosure on a sole member's interest passes the entire interest.
D is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — LLC charging order

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Carroll and Fulton run a trucking business as partners. Carroll bought a $4,600 trailer with money his grandmother lent him, titled it in the business's name, and contributed it to the business. Fulton contributed only labor. They agreed to share profits equally but said nothing about losses. When the business ends, the trailer sells for $4,000. The partnership owes an outside fuel supplier $1,000, and it owes Carroll $500 that he lent it.

Is the trailer partnership property?
o: Yes, because the partners' intent at acquisition, shown by title and use, controls.
No, because the purchase money came from Carroll's grandmother as a personal loan.
No, because Fulton contributed nothing toward buying it.
It is owned by Carroll and Fulton as tenants in common under the UPA.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. These are the In re Fulton facts. The trailer was titled in the business's name, bought for use in the business, and contributed as Carroll's capital.
The source of Carroll's funds does not change the partnership's title and intent.
One partner's contribution can become partnership property.
Under the UPA, specific partnership property is held as tenants in partnership.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Partnership property (Fulton)

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Carroll and Fulton run a trucking business as partners. Carroll bought a $4,600 trailer with money his grandmother lent him, titled it in the business's name, and contributed it to the business. Fulton contributed only labor. They agreed to share profits equally but said nothing about losses. When the business ends, the trailer sells for $4,000. The partnership owes an outside fuel supplier $1,000, and it owes Carroll $500 that he lent it.

Under UPA § 40(b), how is the $4,000 from the sale of the trailer applied?
o: $1,000 to the supplier, then $2,500 toward Carroll's capital, and only then $500 to repay Carroll's loan.
$4,000 to Carroll first, as return of his capital.
$1,000 to the supplier, then $500 to repay Carroll's loan, then $2,500 toward Carroll's $4,600 capital.
$1,000 to the supplier, and the remaining $3,000 split equally between Carroll and Fulton.
None of the above.
oe: Under the UPA, partner loans are repaid before capital.
Outside creditors are always paid first.
Correct. Outside creditors, then partner loans, then capital, then profits.
Loans and capital are paid before anything is split.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — UPA § 40(b) applied

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Carroll and Fulton run a trucking business as partners. Carroll bought a $4,600 trailer with money his grandmother lent him, titled it in the business's name, and contributed it to the business. Fulton contributed only labor. They agreed to share profits equally but said nothing about losses. When the business ends, the trailer sells for $4,000. The partnership owes an outside fuel supplier $1,000, and it owes Carroll $500 that he lent it.

Carroll recovers only $2,500 of his $4,600 capital, leaving a $2,100 shortfall. Applying the UPA's statutory loss-sharing rule (§ 18(a)) rather than Kovacik, how much must Fulton contribute?
oe: That is the Kovacik result.
Correct. Losses are shared like profits (equally), so each partner bears half of the $2,100 capital loss.
Fulton bears only his share.
That is half of the original $4,600 contribution, not half of the loss.
No rule produces this figure.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Statutory loss share

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Carroll and Fulton run a trucking business as partners. Carroll bought a $4,600 trailer with money his grandmother lent him, titled it in the business's name, and contributed it to the business. Fulton contributed only labor. They agreed to share profits equally but said nothing about losses. When the business ends, the trailer sells for $4,000. The partnership owes an outside fuel supplier $1,000, and it owes Carroll $500 that he lent it.

If the court applies Kovacik v. Reed instead, which of the following statements is true?
o: Fulton must contribute $1,050, half of the capital loss.
Fulton must contribute the full $2,100 capital shortfall to Carroll.
Carroll owes Fulton the reasonable value of his labor.
Fulton owes nothing, and Carroll bears the entire $2,100 capital loss.
None of the above.
oe: That is the statutory result.
Not under any rule.
The service partner simply loses the value of his labor.
Correct. Fulton contributed only labor and Carroll only capital, so each loses what he put in.
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Kovacik applied

q:
Q7–11 HYPO: Under the UPA (1914), Carroll and Fulton run a trucking business as partners. Carroll bought a $4,600 trailer with money his grandmother lent him, titled it in the business's name, and contributed it to the business. Fulton contributed only labor. They agreed to share profits equally but said nothing about losses. When the business ends, the trailer sells for $4,000. The partnership owes an outside fuel supplier $1,000, and it owes Carroll $500 that he lent it.

Fulton files for personal bankruptcy, and his bankruptcy estate claims the trailer. Which of the following statements is true?
o: Fulton's estate takes the trailer, because Fulton co-owned it as a partner.
Fulton's estate takes half the trailer.
The trailer goes to Fulton's personal creditors before partnership creditors are paid.
Carroll must buy the trailer from Fulton's estate.
Fulton's estate gets only his partnership interest, not the trailer itself.
oe: The partnership owns the trailer; a partner's creditors cannot reach specific partnership property.
The trailer is not divided between the partners.
Partnership creditors are paid from partnership assets first.
The estate does not own the trailer.
Correct. In re Fulton: the bankrupt partner's estate gets only his partnership interest, meaning his share of any distributions, not the trailer.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Partner's bankruptcy

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Wade, Xena, and Yuri are partners in a partnership that owns a shopping center, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until the center's ground lease ends in 2045. In 2027 the business loses money. Wade stops contributing his share of required funding and then sues to dissolve the partnership because of the losses.

Under Collins v. Lewis, how should the court rule on Wade's suit to dissolve the partnership?
o: It should order dissolution, because the partnership is losing money.
It should order dissolution, because any partner may dissolve a partnership at any time without liability.
It should deny dissolution, because Wade's own conduct caused the losses.
It should deny dissolution, because a partnership for a term can never be dissolved before the term ends.
None of the above.
oe: Losses alone, especially losses caused by the complaining partner, do not justify dissolution.
A partner has the power, but not always the right, to dissolve.

Correct. Wade has the power, but not the right, to dissolve before the term ends, and a wrongful dissolution makes him liable for damages. This is the source of the power-versus-right rule (RUPA § 602(a)).
A court may dissolve on statutory grounds, and a partner always has the power to withdraw.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Collins v. Lewis

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Wade, Xena, and Yuri are partners in a partnership that owns a shopping center, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until the center's ground lease ends in 2045. In 2027 the business loses money. Wade stops contributing his share of required funding and then sues to dissolve the partnership because of the losses.

Assume a court orders the partnership dissolved and its property sold at a judicial sale. Xena and Yuri want to bid on the property. Wade objects that they froze him out. Under Prentiss v. Sheffel, which of the following statements is true?
o: Xena and Yuri may bid, absent proof of a bad-faith plan to freeze Wade out.
Majority partners may never bid at their own partnership's dissolution sale.
They may bid only if they pay at least the appraised value of the property.
Only outside bidders may participate, to protect the minority partner.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Their bid may raise the price and increase Wade's share. That is how judicial sales work in winding up.
Prentiss allowed it.
No such rule exists.
Partners may bid.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Prentiss v. Sheffel

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Wade, Xena, and Yuri are partners in a partnership that owns a shopping center, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until the center's ground lease ends in 2045. In 2027 the business loses money. Wade stops contributing his share of required funding and then sues to dissolve the partnership because of the losses.

Suppose instead that the court lets Xena buy out Wade's interest rather than ordering a sale. Under Disotell v. Stiltner, which of the following statements is true?
o: A court may never order a buyout instead of a liquidation sale.
The buyout price may be set at whatever the court thinks fair, without evidence.
Wade need not account for his personal use of partnership property during winding up.
A buyout is allowed, but only at fair market value proven by evidence.
None of the above.
oe: Disotell allowed a buyout.
The price must be proven by evidence.
A partner must account for personal use of partnership property.
Correct. Disotell marks the shift from forced liquidation to buyouts (now RUPA § 701).
D is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Disotell v. Stiltner

q:
Q12–15 HYPO: Wade, Xena, and Yuri are partners in a partnership that owns a shopping center, governed by the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997). Their written agreement says the partnership will last until the center's ground lease ends in 2045. In 2027 the business loses money. Wade stops contributing his share of required funding and then sues to dissolve the partnership because of the losses.

In 2028, Wade's personal judgment creditor obtains a charging order against Wade's transferable interest. When may the creditor, as a transferee, ask a court to dissolve the partnership?
o: At any time, because the charging order makes the creditor a transferee.
Only after the term ends in 2045, and only if the court finds winding up equitable.
Never, because a transferee has no rights at all against the partnership itself.
Immediately, because the charging order dissociates Wade from the firm.
None of the above.
oe: That applies only if the partnership was at will when the charging order was entered.

Correct. RUPA § 801: a transferee may seek dissolution after the term expires (term partnership) or at any time (at-will partnership). The partnership was for a term when the charging order was entered.
A transferee has this limited dissolution right.
A charging order does not dissociate the partner.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Transferee's dissolution right
